questions.stem: A 6-month-old boy is evaluated for poor feeding, failure to thrive, and developmental delay. Examination shows low-set ears, a small chin, and a heart murmur; echocardiography reveals a ventricular septal defect. The physician suspects a microdeletion syndrome and wants a test targeted to a single known genomic region. Which technique is most appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fluorescence in situ hybridization

choices.label: B
choices.text: G-banded karyotype read at 550-band resolution

choices.label: C
choices.text: Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) of patient DNA

choices.label: D
choices.text: Serum karyotype of both parents to look for a balanced rearrangement

choices.label: E
choices.text: Southern blot with a radiolabeled probe

explanation.summary: FISH is a targeted, a priori method ideal for confirming a suspected microdeletion such as 22q11.
explanation.whyCorrect: The presentation (conotruncal heart defect, dysmorphism) suggests DiGeorge (22q11.2 deletion) syndrome. FISH uses a fluorescent probe designed for a known locus, so it can confirm a specific suspected microdeletion that is below the resolution of routine karyotyping.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A standard G-banded karyotype only resolves abnormalities larger than about 5-10 Mb and cannot detect a microdeletion.
whyWrongByChoice.C: PCR amplifies DNA but is only one step in a genotyping workflow and does not by itself localize a chromosomal microdeletion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Parental karyotypes evaluate recurrent pregnancy loss and would not detect the child's submicroscopic deletion.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Southern blot is a low-throughput historic method requiring large amounts of DNA and a radiolabeled probe; it is not the modern choice for a microdeletion.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (1 of 3) - Cytogenetics

questions.stem: A 2-month-old girl has poor feeding, recurrent vomiting, and failure to thrive. Examination shows microcephaly, epicanthal folds, and a cardiac murmur, and echocardiography reveals a ventricular septal defect. A G-banded karyotype is reported as normal 46,XX. Which technique is most likely to establish the diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Array comparative genomic hybridization

choices.label: B
choices.text: Northern blot of peripheral blood RNA

choices.label: C
choices.text: Repeat G-banded karyotype at higher resolution

choices.label: D
choices.text: Southern blot with a locus-specific probe

choices.label: E
choices.text: Western blot of a lymphocyte lysate

explanation.summary: Array CGH is an unbiased, genome-wide test that detects submicroscopic copy number variants missed by karyotyping.
explanation.whyCorrect: With a normal karyotype but strong clinical suspicion of a congenital syndrome, array CGH can scan the whole genome and detect a small deletion (for example a ~1.5 Mb 7q11.23 deletion causing Williams syndrome) down to roughly 50-200 kb.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Northern blot detects RNA transcripts, not chromosomal copy number changes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Repeating the karyotype adds nothing, since a deletion this small is below its 5-10 Mb resolution.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Southern blot is a targeted method for a known locus and cannot survey the genome for an unknown deletion.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Western blot detects proteins and cannot identify a genomic deletion.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (1 of 3) - Cytogenetics

questions.stem: A genetics laboratory runs array CGH on a patient's DNA labeled with a red fluorophore against reference DNA labeled with a green fluorophore. At one microarray well, the scanner reports a fluorescence signal that is predominantly green. What does this finding indicate at that locus?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A balanced translocation

choices.label: B
choices.text: A deletion in the patient's DNA

choices.label: C
choices.text: A duplication in the patient's DNA

choices.label: D
choices.text: A point mutation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Normal copy number

explanation.summary: In array CGH a green-dominant (weak red) signal means the patient's test DNA failed to bind, implying a deletion.
explanation.whyCorrect: Test DNA is red and reference DNA is green. A weaker red signal relative to green means less patient DNA hybridized at that locus, indicating the sequence is deleted in the patient.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Array CGH cannot detect balanced translocations because copy number is unchanged.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A duplication would give a stronger red (test) signal, not a predominantly green one.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Array CGH measures copy number, not single-base substitutions.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Normal copy number gives equal red and green, seen as a yellow signal.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (1 of 3) - Cytogenetics

questions.stem: During karyotype preparation, cultured cells are treated with colchicine before the chromosomes are spread onto a slide. What is the purpose of this step?

choices.label: A
choices.text: To arrest cell division at metaphase

choices.label: B
choices.text: To denature DNA into single strands

choices.label: C
choices.text: To digest histone proteins

choices.label: D
choices.text: To fluorescently label the probe

choices.label: E
choices.text: To stain AT-rich regions

explanation.summary: Colchicine arrests dividing cells in metaphase, when chromosomes are most condensed and best visualized.
explanation.whyCorrect: Colchicine disrupts spindle microtubules and halts mitosis at metaphase, where chromosomes are maximally condensed, defined, and aligned at the equator, making them ideal for analysis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Denaturation into single strands is a step in FISH, not chromosome arrest.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Partial digestion of histones is done later with the protease trypsin, not colchicine.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Fluorescent labeling applies to FISH probes, not to metaphase arrest.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Staining of AT-rich regions is achieved with Giemsa, which produces dark bands.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (1 of 3) - Cytogenetics

questions.stem: A G-banded karyotype shows a chromosome region that stains as a dark band with Giemsa. Which description best characterizes this dark (G-positive) band?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A centromeric copy number gain

choices.label: B
choices.text: A region of active DNA replication

choices.label: C
choices.text: A site of a balanced translocation

choices.label: D
choices.text: AT-rich, gene-poor heterochromatin

choices.label: E
choices.text: GC-rich, gene-rich euchromatin with active transcription

explanation.summary: Dark G-positive bands are AT-rich, gene-poor heterochromatin where Giemsa binds strongly.
explanation.whyCorrect: Giemsa binds more strongly to AT-rich DNA, producing dark bands that correspond to gene-poor heterochromatin. Light G-negative bands are GC-rich, gene-rich euchromatin.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Band color reflects DNA composition, not copy number changes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Banding reflects base composition and chromatin state, not sites of active replication.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A dark band is a normal staining feature, not evidence of a translocation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: GC-rich, gene-rich euchromatin corresponds to light (G-negative) bands, not dark bands.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (1 of 3) - Cytogenetics

questions.stem: A karyotype from a male patient shows the short arm of chromosome 9 and the short arm of chromosome 22 exchanging material, with both chromosomes 9 and 22 altered and a normal Y chromosome present. Which abnormality is best described by these findings?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Trisomy 21

choices.label: E
choices.text: 45,X (Turner syndrome)

explanation.summary: Involvement of two chromosomes (9 and 22) exchanging material indicates a reciprocal translocation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because two different chromosomes are altered, the finding is a translocation, t(9;22). A deletion, duplication, or aneuploidy each involves only a single chromosome or chromosome count.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Trisomy 21 involves an extra chromosome 21, not an exchange between chromosomes 9 and 22.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A del(22) involves only chromosome 22, but here two chromosomes are affected.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A dup(22) affects only one chromosome and would not be visible as an exchange between two.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 45,X (Turner syndrome) is excluded because a Y chromosome is visible in a male patient.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (1 of 3) - Cytogenetics

questions.stem: A 13-year-old boy has progressive gait and limb ataxia, dysarthria, and cardiomyopathy. Genetic testing shows a very large GAA trinucleotide repeat expansion in intron 1 of the FXN gene that is too long to size reliably by conventional PCR. Which technique is best suited to accurately size this expansion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Array CGH

choices.label: B
choices.text: FISH

choices.label: C
choices.text: G-banded karyotype

choices.label: D
choices.text: Southern blot

choices.label: E
choices.text: Western blot

explanation.summary: Southern blot can accurately size very large repeat expansions that exceed the limits of conventional PCR.
explanation.whyCorrect: The clinical picture is Friedreich ataxia, caused by a GAA expansion in FXN. Southern blotting analyzes genomic DNA directly after restriction digestion and can size large expansions (as in Friedreich ataxia or myotonic dystrophy type 1) that are too long for standard PCR.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Array CGH detects copy number variants and would not size a repeat expansion.
whyWrongByChoice.B: FISH detects copy number and location of a locus, not the length of a repeat expansion.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A karyotype cannot resolve a trinucleotide repeat expansion within a gene.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Western blot detects proteins, not DNA repeat length.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (1 of 3) - Cytogenetics

questions.stem: A student asks why FISH is described as a targeted or a priori method. Which statement best explains this characteristic?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It can only be performed on interphase nuclei

choices.label: B
choices.text: It detects copy number variants across the whole genome without assumptions

choices.label: C
choices.text: It fluorescently labels the entire genome at once

choices.label: D
choices.text: It measures a red-to-green fluorescence ratio

choices.label: E
choices.text: It requires prior knowledge of the suspected abnormality to design a probe

explanation.summary: FISH only reveals suspected abnormalities because a probe must be designed for a known target sequence.
explanation.whyCorrect: FISH is targeted: the probe is a short single-stranded DNA sequence complementary to a specific locus. Because the probe must be designed in advance, FISH requires prior knowledge of the suspected abnormality and detects only what it was designed to find.

whyWrongByChoice.A: FISH can be performed on metaphase chromosomes or interphase nuclei.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Unbiased genome-wide, assumption-free detection describes array CGH, not FISH.
whyWrongByChoice.C: FISH labels specific target sequences, not the entire genome indiscriminately.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The red-to-green fluorescence ratio is the readout of array CGH, not FISH.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (1 of 3) - Cytogenetics

questions.stem: A couple with recurrent pregnancy loss is referred for evaluation. The clinician explains that a particular class of chromosomal abnormality is over-represented in this setting and can be identified by testing the chromosomes of each partner. Which technique is used for this evaluation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Array CGH

choices.label: B
choices.text: G-banded karyotype

choices.label: C
choices.text: PCR

choices.label: D
choices.text: Southern blot

choices.label: E
choices.text: Western blot

explanation.summary: Karyotype testing of couples detects balanced translocations, a major cause of recurrent pregnancy loss.
explanation.whyCorrect: Karyotype testing is part of the evaluation of recurrent pregnancy loss because balanced reciprocal and Robertsonian translocations are the major abnormalities identified, and these balanced rearrangements are visible on a karyotype.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Array CGH cannot detect balanced translocations because they do not change copy number.
whyWrongByChoice.C: PCR amplifies specific sequences and does not visualize whole-chromosome rearrangements.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Southern blot is a targeted single-locus method, not a survey for translocations.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Western blot detects proteins and is irrelevant to chromosomal rearrangements.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (1 of 3) - Cytogenetics

questions.stem: A clinician wants an unbiased test that scans the entire genome for copy number variants as small as approximately 50-200 kilobases in a child with intellectual disability. However, the clinician is warned that the test cannot detect one important type of abnormality. Which abnormality will this test miss?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A balanced reciprocal translocation

choices.label: B
choices.text: A duplication of a 200-kilobase genomic segment

choices.label: C
choices.text: A heterozygous 100-kilobase microdeletion

choices.label: D
choices.text: A homozygous deletion of an entire gene

choices.label: E
choices.text: A three-copy duplication of one gene

explanation.summary: Array CGH is high-resolution and genome-wide but cannot detect balanced rearrangements.
explanation.whyCorrect: Array CGH measures copy number, so it detects deletions and duplications genome-wide. A balanced reciprocal translocation does not change the amount of DNA, so it produces a normal (yellow) ratio and is missed.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A duplication increases copy number and gives a red-dominant signal on array CGH.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A heterozygous microdeletion reduces copy number and is readily detected by array CGH.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A homozygous deletion is a strong copy number loss and is detected by array CGH.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A three-copy duplication is a copy number gain and is detected as a +1 dosage change.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (1 of 3) - Cytogenetics

questions.stem: A FISH assay for the 22q11 region uses two probes: an ARSA control probe (green) located outside the deleted region and a TUPLE1 probe (red) located at 22q11. In the patient's cells, two green signals are seen but only one red signal is observed. What does this result indicate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A 22q11 duplication on one homolog

choices.label: B
choices.text: A heterozygous 22q11 deletion

choices.label: C
choices.text: A homozygous 22q11 deletion on both homologs

choices.label: D
choices.text: A normal 22q11 region on both copies

choices.label: E
choices.text: Trisomy 22 with three chromosome copies

explanation.summary: One red signal with two control signals indicates loss of one copy of the target region, a heterozygous deletion.
explanation.whyCorrect: The control (green) probe marks both copies of chromosome 22, while the target (red) probe marks 22q11. Two green signals confirm both chromosomes 22 are present; a single red signal shows the 22q11 region is missing on one of them, a heterozygous deletion.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A duplication would produce an extra red signal, not a reduced number.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A homozygous deletion would show no red signal at all, not one.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A normal region would show two red signals matching the two green controls.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Trisomy 22 would show three green control signals from three copies of chromosome 22.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (1 of 3) - Cytogenetics

questions.stem: A 4-year-old girl with developmental delay is evaluated. The physician wants a single test that can visualize all chromosomes arranged in pairs to assess both chromosome number and gross structure. Which technique meets this description?

choices.label: A
choices.text: FISH

choices.label: B
choices.text: Karyotyping

choices.label: C
choices.text: PCR

choices.label: D
choices.text: SNP microarray

choices.label: E
choices.text: Southern blot

explanation.summary: Karyotyping visualizes all chromosomes in pairs to assess number and structure.
explanation.whyCorrect: A karyotype arranges all chromosomes into pairs by size and banding pattern (1-22 plus the sex chromosomes), allowing assessment of both numerical and gross structural abnormalities in a single view.

whyWrongByChoice.A: FISH targets specific loci with probes and does not display all chromosomes as pairs.
whyWrongByChoice.C: PCR amplifies specific DNA sequences and does not visualize chromosomes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A SNP microarray detects single-nucleotide polymorphisms and copy number, not a whole-chromosome image.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Southern blot analyzes a specific DNA fragment and cannot visualize whole chromosomes.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (1 of 3) - Cytogenetics

questions.stem: A research laboratory is optimizing a polymerase chain reaction (PCR) protocol in which the reaction mixture is repeatedly heated to 95 degrees C to separate the DNA strands. The technicians note that, unlike DNA polymerases isolated from animal cells, the enzyme they use remains active after each high-temperature step. From which organism was this enzyme most likely purified?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Escherichia coli, a mesophilic gut bacterium

choices.label: B
choices.text: Homo sapiens, using native cellular polymerase

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mycobacterium tuberculosis, an acid-fast bacillus

choices.label: D
choices.text: Saccharomyces cerevisiae, a budding yeast

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thermus aquaticus, a thermophilic bacterium

explanation.summary: PCR relies on the heat-stable Taq polymerase, which comes from a thermophilic bacterium.
explanation.whyCorrect: Taq polymerase was purified from Thermus aquaticus, a bacterium that lives in hot environments (50 to 80 degrees C) such as hot springs. Because it is heat-stable, it stays active even after repeated exposure to the ~95 degrees C denaturation step, which made automated PCR possible.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Escherichia coli polymerase is not heat-stable and would be denatured by the 95 degrees C step, requiring fresh enzyme each cycle.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Human DNA polymerases are heat-labile; the brick notes Arthur Kornberg discovered the human enzyme, but it is not heat-stable.
whyWrongByChoice.C: M. tuberculosis DNA can be detected by PCR, but it is not the source of the thermostable enzyme.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Yeast is not the source of the thermostable polymerase used in PCR.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (2 of 3), DNA analysis

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy of West African descent presents with recurrent vaso-occlusive pain crises and anemia. To genotype his HBB gene, his amplified DNA is digested with the restriction enzyme DdeI, which recognizes the sequence CTNAG. The gel shows a single undigested band, identical to the pre-digestion product. Which of the following best explains this result?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A point mutation abolished the DdeI recognition site

choices.label: B
choices.text: A point mutation created a new DdeI recognition site

choices.label: C
choices.text: He is a heterozygous carrier with one normal and one mutant allele

choices.label: D
choices.text: The DNA contains a large insertion within the amplified fragment

choices.label: E
choices.text: The PCR failed to amplify the target region

explanation.summary: In sickle cell disease the HBB point mutation destroys the DdeI restriction site, leaving the fragment uncut.
explanation.whyCorrect: Sickle cell disease is caused by a point mutation in HBB (c.20A>T, p.Glu7Val) that replaces adenine with thymine. This change alters the CTNAG recognition sequence so DdeI can no longer cut. A homozygous mutant (HbSS) patient therefore shows a single, undigested band of the full PCR-product size.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A new site would produce additional (smaller) cut fragments, not a single uncut band; the mutation removes rather than adds a site.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A heterozygous carrier (HbAS) shows three bands, one uncut and two digested, not a single uncut band.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A large insertion would produce a larger band than the reference product; here the band matches the undigested PCR product size.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A failed PCR would show no band at all, not a full-length product.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (2 of 3), DNA analysis

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man is diagnosed with colorectal cancer and has a family history of multiple relatives with early-onset colorectal and endometrial cancers, raising concern for Lynch syndrome. His clinician wants to screen the five genes commonly implicated (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2, and EPCAM) in a single test. Which of the following is the most appropriate molecular technique?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH)

choices.label: B
choices.text: Karyotyping

choices.label: C
choices.text: Next-generation sequencing multigene panel

choices.label: D
choices.text: Restriction fragment length polymorphism analysis

choices.label: E
choices.text: SNP-microarray

explanation.summary: Sequencing several disease genes at once is best done with a targeted NGS gene panel.
explanation.whyCorrect: An NGS panel of the mismatch-repair genes sequences MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2, and EPCAM simultaneously, generally covering the exons and exon-intron (splicing) boundaries where causative mutations lie. If no mutation is found, an untargeted exome or genome approach can follow.

whyWrongByChoice.A: FISH detects specific chromosomal loci or rearrangements, not sequence-level mutations across a gene panel.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Karyotyping detects large chromosomal abnormalities, not single-gene point mutations.
whyWrongByChoice.D: RFLP only detects a specific known mutation that alters a restriction site, not the full spectrum of mutations across five genes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: SNP-arrays detect only common known variants for which probes exist and would miss rare or novel mutations.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (2 of 3), DNA analysis

questions.stem: A genetics laboratory runs a SNP-microarray on a patient with a strong clinical suspicion of a rare, previously unreported single-nucleotide variant. The array returns a normal result, yet the patient is later found to carry a pathogenic novel variant. Which inherent property of SNP-microarrays best explains this false-negative result?

choices.label: A
choices.text: SNP-arrays are more expensive than whole-genome sequencing per sample tested

choices.label: B
choices.text: SNP-arrays cannot detect copy number variations or loss of heterozygosity

choices.label: C
choices.text: SNP-arrays only detect variants for which a probe is present on the chip

choices.label: D
choices.text: SNP-arrays require a heat-stable polymerase that denatures the patient sample

choices.label: E
choices.text: SNP-arrays sequence the entire genome base by base at low read depth

explanation.summary: SNP-arrays are a targeted approach and only detect variants represented by probes on the chip.
explanation.whyCorrect: SNP-microarrays function as genotyping panels that interrogate only pre-selected regions. They can detect a variant only if a probe for it is present, so rare or novel variants not represented on the chip are missed.

whyWrongByChoice.A: SNP-arrays are described as cost-effective and less expensive than sequencing, not more expensive.
whyWrongByChoice.B: SNP-arrays actually can detect copy number variations and loss of heterozygosity in addition to SNPs.
whyWrongByChoice.D: SNP-arrays are hybridization-based genotyping panels; the heat-stable polymerase description applies to PCR, not to why the array missed the variant.
whyWrongByChoice.E: SNP-arrays do not sequence the genome; they are a targeted probe-based method, which is precisely why novel variants are missed.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (2 of 3), DNA analysis

questions.stem: A child with cystic fibrosis tests negative for the common F508del CFTR mutation on a SNP-array, but clinical suspicion remains high. Because roughly 30% of disease-causing CFTR variants are not detected by the array, the clinician wants to comprehensively analyze the entire CFTR gene for additional pathogenic mutations. Which technique is most appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fluorescence in situ hybridization

choices.label: B
choices.text: Karyotyping

choices.label: C
choices.text: Repeat the SNP-array with a different platform

choices.label: D
choices.text: Restriction enzyme digestion for F508del

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sanger sequencing of the CFTR gene

explanation.summary: Sequencing is required to comprehensively read a gene and detect mutations beyond common variants.
explanation.whyCorrect: SNP-arrays detect the common F508del mutation but miss up to 30% of disease-causing variants. Sanger sequencing reads the DNA base by base and enables comprehensive analysis of the entire CFTR gene to identify additional pathogenic mutations.

whyWrongByChoice.A: FISH visualizes chromosomal loci, not the base-level sequence of the CFTR gene.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Karyotyping evaluates chromosome-level abnormalities, not single-base CFTR mutations.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Repeating a targeted array with different probe content still only detects variants represented on the chip, not the full gene.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Restriction digestion only interrogates the specific F508del site, which already tested negative, and cannot survey the whole gene.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (2 of 3), DNA analysis

questions.stem: During a Sanger sequencing reaction, DNA synthesis stops at specific bases, generating a collection of fragments of varying lengths that each end with a labeled terminal nucleotide. Which property of the special nucleotides added to the reaction is responsible for terminating chain elongation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They are present at a higher concentration than standard dNTPs

choices.label: B
choices.text: They bind the primer and block its annealing to the template

choices.label: C
choices.text: They carry an extra phosphate group that repels the polymerase

choices.label: D
choices.text: They cause the DNA polymerase to become permanently denatured

choices.label: E
choices.text: They lack a 3-prime hydroxyl group

explanation.summary: Dideoxynucleotides terminate Sanger sequencing because they lack a 3-prime hydroxyl group.
explanation.whyCorrect: Sanger sequencing uses fluorochrome-labeled dideoxynucleotides (ddNTPs) that act as chain-elongating inhibitors. Unlike dNTPs, ddNTPs lack a 3-prime hydroxyl group, so once incorporated they cannot form a phosphodiester bond with the next nucleotide, terminating synthesis at that base.

whyWrongByChoice.A: ddNTPs are present at much lower concentration than dNTPs, so they incorporate randomly rather than at every position.
whyWrongByChoice.B: ddNTPs are incorporated into the growing strand by the polymerase; they do not block primer annealing.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Chain termination results from the missing 3-prime OH, not from an extra phosphate repelling the enzyme.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The polymerase is not denatured; it simply cannot extend past an incorporated ddNTP.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (2 of 3), DNA analysis

questions.stem: A student loads DNA fragments of several sizes into a single well of an agarose gel and applies an electric current. After running the gel, which of the following fragments will have migrated farthest from the well toward the positive electrode?

choices.label: A
choices.text: All fragments migrate equally regardless of size, because charge is uniform

choices.label: B
choices.text: Only uncut fragments migrate; digested fragments remain trapped in the well

choices.label: C
choices.text: The fragment closest to the negative electrode migrates farthest down the gel

choices.label: D
choices.text: The largest fragment, because it carries the most negative charge overall

choices.label: E
choices.text: The smallest fragment, because it passes through the gel pores most easily

explanation.summary: In gel electrophoresis smaller DNA fragments migrate faster and travel farther than larger ones.
explanation.whyCorrect: Electrophoresis separates charged DNA molecules that migrate toward the positive electrode in an electric field. Small fragments pass through the gel pores more easily and migrate faster, so they travel the farthest, while larger fragments move more slowly and stay closer to the well.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Fragments are separated precisely because migration depends on size.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Both cut and uncut fragments migrate; their distance depends on their size.
whyWrongByChoice.C: DNA is negatively charged and migrates toward the positive electrode; proximity to the negative electrode does not determine distance traveled.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Migration is governed by size-dependent movement through the pores, not by larger fragments carrying more charge; larger fragments move more slowly.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (2 of 3), DNA analysis

questions.stem: A patient's Sanger sequencing electropherogram is reviewed. At one position, instead of a single clean peak, two overlapping peaks of different colors are seen at the same location, while the rest of the trace shows clear single peaks. Which of the following does this finding most likely indicate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A heterozygous variant at that position

choices.label: B
choices.text: A homozygous mutant genotype at that position

choices.label: C
choices.text: A homozygous wild-type genotype at that position

choices.label: D
choices.text: A large chromosomal deletion spanning the gene

choices.label: E
choices.text: Complete failure of the sequencing reaction

explanation.summary: Overlapping electropherogram peaks at one position reflect a heterozygous variant.
explanation.whyCorrect: Each electropherogram peak represents a single nucleotide, and clear non-overlapping peaks indicate a reliable base call. Overlapping peaks at one position indicate a mixed signal from two different bases, characteristic of a heterozygous individual carrying two different alleles.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A homozygous mutant position also gives a single clean peak, just of a different base.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A homozygous wild-type position gives a single clean peak, not overlapping peaks.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A large deletion is not detected as overlapping single-base peaks on a Sanger electropherogram.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A failed reaction would produce no readable peaks, not two clear overlapping ones at a single position.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (2 of 3), DNA analysis

questions.stem: A clinician needs to detect a completely novel point mutation in a patient whose disease gene is unknown from prior testing. Which of the following techniques is capable of detecting novel point mutations?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Array comparative genomic hybridization (aCGH)

choices.label: B
choices.text: DNA sequencing

choices.label: C
choices.text: PCR alone

choices.label: D
choices.text: Restriction enzyme digestion

choices.label: E
choices.text: SNP-array

explanation.summary: Only sequencing can detect novel point mutations, because it reads previously unknown bases directly.
explanation.whyCorrect: DNA sequencing, whether Sanger (after PCR) or NGS, reads the sequence base by base and can identify point mutations that were not previously characterized. The other listed methods are targeted approaches limited to known variants or serve a different purpose.

whyWrongByChoice.A: aCGH is designed to detect copy number variations, not point mutations.
whyWrongByChoice.C: PCR only amplifies DNA and must be combined with another technique to detect mutations.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Restriction enzyme digestion detects only known mutations that alter a restriction site, not novel variants.
whyWrongByChoice.E: SNP-arrays are targeted and detect only well-characterized variants with existing probes, not novel ones.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (2 of 3), DNA analysis

questions.stem: A pathologist wants to detect a somatic mutation that is present in only a small proportion of cells within a tissue biopsy, a situation of low-level mosaicism. Which feature of next-generation sequencing best enables detection of such rare, low-frequency variants?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Deep coverage, in which each base is read many times

choices.label: B
choices.text: Karyotyping the mosaic cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reading each base only once to save cost

choices.label: D
choices.text: Restricting analysis to a single restriction site

choices.label: E
choices.text: Using dideoxynucleotides to terminate every strand

explanation.summary: Deep NGS coverage, reading each base many times, is what allows detection of rare low-frequency variants.
explanation.whyCorrect: Deep coverage means each base is read many times, which enhances the ability to detect rare mutations such as those seen in mosaicism. Somatic mutations present in only a small fraction of cells could be missed if coverage is insufficient; ultra-deep sequencing reads a base thousands of times for even rarer targets.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Karyotyping detects large chromosomal abnormalities, not low-frequency single-nucleotide somatic mutations.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Reading each base only once (shallow coverage) would likely miss low-frequency variants.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Analyzing a single restriction site is an RFLP concept and cannot survey rare somatic variants across a region.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Dideoxynucleotides are used in Sanger sequencing and do not confer NGS's deep-coverage sensitivity for mosaicism.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (2 of 3), DNA analysis

questions.stem: A technician is setting up the temperature program on a thermal cycler for PCR. She needs to select the step during which the two short oligonucleotide primers bind to their complementary sequences on the single-stranded template. Which step and approximate temperature range is she programming?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Annealing at 50 to 65 degrees C

choices.label: B
choices.text: Denaturation at 95 degrees C

choices.label: C
choices.text: Elongation at 72 degrees C

choices.label: D
choices.text: Final hold at 4 degrees C

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ligation at 16 degrees C

explanation.summary: Primers bind the template during the annealing step at roughly 50 to 65 degrees C.
explanation.whyCorrect: A PCR cycle is divided into steps defined by temperature. During annealing (about 50 to 65 degrees C, 20 to 40 seconds), the forward and reverse primers bind to their complementary sequences on the separated single strands, defining the fragment to be amplified.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Denaturation at 95 degrees C separates the double strand into single strands; primers do not bind at this temperature.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Elongation at 72 degrees C is when Taq polymerase extends the new strand from the already-bound primers.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A 4 degrees C hold is a post-reaction storage step, not the primer-binding step.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ligation is not a step of the standard PCR cycle described in this technique.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (2 of 3), DNA analysis

questions.stem: A patient with acute leukemia relapses after initial treatment. A molecular study of the relapse sample reveals uniparental disomy at the 19p13.3-p12 locus and altered allele-specific gene dosage that were not present at initial diagnosis. Which technique was most likely used to generate these genotyping data?

choices.label: A
choices.text: PCR alone

choices.label: B
choices.text: Restriction enzyme digestion

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sanger sequencing

choices.label: D
choices.text: SNP-microarray

choices.label: E
choices.text: Standard karyotyping

explanation.summary: SNP-arrays reveal allele-specific dosage, copy number, and uniparental disomy, useful in comparing diagnosis to relapse.
explanation.whyCorrect: SNP-microarrays detect SNPs, copy number variations, and loss of heterozygosity, and they report total and allele-specific gene dosage. This allows detection of uniparental disomy, which the brick illustrates as being seen only at relapse when comparing an initial tumor to a relapse tumor.

whyWrongByChoice.A: PCR alone amplifies DNA and does not by itself produce dosage or genotype plots.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Restriction digestion only assesses a single known restriction site, not genome-wide dosage or LOH.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Sanger sequencing reads base-by-base sequence but does not generate genome-wide allele-specific dosage or detect uniparental disomy across a locus.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Standard karyotyping detects large structural changes but cannot reveal copy-neutral uniparental disomy or allele-specific dosage.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (2 of 3), DNA analysis

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman is about to begin a medication for which patients show highly variable responses. Before prescribing, her physician orders a genetic test to personalize treatment, predict drug efficacy, and minimize the risk of adverse drug reactions. Which of the following techniques is most appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Agarose gel electrophoresis of a PCR product

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fluorescence in situ hybridization of a metaphase spread

choices.label: C
choices.text: Karyotyping of peripheral blood lymphocytes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pharmacogenomic SNP-array

choices.label: E
choices.text: Restriction enzyme digestion of the HBB gene

explanation.summary: Pharmacogenomic SNP arrays detect SNPs associated with variable drug responses.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pharmacogenomic SNP arrays are used to detect SNPs associated with variable responses to certain medications. This information is used to personalize treatment, predict drug efficacy, and potentially minimize adverse drug reactions, which is exactly the goal here.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Gel electrophoresis only separates DNA fragments by size and does not reveal sequence variants.
whyWrongByChoice.B: FISH shows the presence, absence, or location of specific DNA sequences on chromosomes, not pharmacogenomic SNPs.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Karyotyping detects large chromosomal abnormalities and provides no information on single-nucleotide variants that alter drug response.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Restriction digestion of HBB genotypes a single known mutation (the sickle cell variant) and is unrelated to drug-response SNPs.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (2 of 3), DNA analysis

questions.stem: Investigators enroll several thousand participants with Type II diabetes and several thousand unaffected controls in order to associate genetic variation across the genome with disease susceptibility. Which of the following is the most appropriate genotyping technique for this genome-wide association study?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Array comparative genomic hybridization

choices.label: B
choices.text: Karyotyping

choices.label: C
choices.text: Restriction fragment length polymorphism analysis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sanger sequencing of a single candidate gene

choices.label: E
choices.text: SNP-microarray

explanation.summary: SNP-arrays are widely used in genome-wide association studies and detect susceptibility variants for complex diseases.
explanation.whyCorrect: SNP-microarrays evaluate a large number of variants across the genome in a single, cost-effective test. They are widely used in GWAS to associate genetic variation with diseases or traits and can detect susceptibility variants for complex diseases such as Alzheimer's or Type II diabetes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: aCGH is designed to detect copy number variations, not the single-nucleotide variants used in GWAS.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Karyotyping detects large structural or numerical chromosomal abnormalities, not single-nucleotide susceptibility variants.
whyWrongByChoice.C: RFLP interrogates a single known mutation that alters a restriction site, not genome-wide variation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sanger sequencing reads one selected region base by base; it cannot survey genome-wide variation in thousands of participants.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (2 of 3), DNA analysis

questions.stem: A patient's DNA is analyzed with SNP-arrays from two different manufacturers. Platform 1 reports a heterozygous variant in a gene of interest, whereas platform 2 reports no variant at that locus. Repeat runs give the same results on each platform, and Sanger sequencing confirms that the variant is present. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for the discrepancy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Platform 2 used a heat-labile DNA polymerase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Probe content differs between the two array platforms

choices.label: C
choices.text: The sample sent to platform 2 contained a large deletion

choices.label: D
choices.text: The variant arose de novo between the two runs

choices.label: E
choices.text: The variant is novel and absent from every database

explanation.summary: Probe content varies between SNP-array platforms, so not all arrays test for the same variants.
explanation.whyCorrect: SNP-arrays can only detect variants for which probes are present on the chip. Because probe content varies between platforms, not all arrays test for the same variants (although there is usually overlap for well-characterized mutations). Platform 2 simply lacks a probe for this variant.

whyWrongByChoice.A: SNP-arrays are hybridization-based genotyping panels; the heat-stable polymerase issue belongs to PCR and does not explain a missing probe.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A large deletion would not be confined to one platform's result, and Sanger sequencing confirmed the variant is present in the sample.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The same DNA sample gives reproducible results on each platform; a de novo change between runs would not produce a consistent platform-specific discrepancy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A truly novel variant would be missed by both arrays, since neither would carry a probe for it; platform 1 detected it.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (2 of 3), DNA analysis

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man with cystic fibrosis, homozygous for the F508del mutation in CFTR, presents with his partner for infertility evaluation. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his infertility?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism from pituitary failure

choices.label: C
choices.text: Retrograde ejaculation into the urinary bladder

choices.label: D
choices.text: Testicular atrophy from chronic pulmonary hypoxia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Varicocele with impaired spermatogenesis

explanation.summary: Almost all males with cystic fibrosis are infertile because of congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cystic fibrosis (mucoviscidosis) is characterized by thick mucus leading to the triad of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, exocrine pancreatic insufficiency, and elevated sodium and chloride in sweat. Almost all males with CF are infertile due to congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Male infertility in CF is a structural absence of the vas deferens, not a hormonal deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Retrograde ejaculation is not the mechanism described for CF-related infertility.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Testicular atrophy from hypoxia is not the cause; the vas deferens is congenitally absent.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Varicocele is not the CF-associated cause of infertility.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (2 of 3), DNA analysis

questions.stem: A 3-month-old girl has recurrent pulmonary infections, steatorrhea from exocrine pancreatic insufficiency, and an elevated sweat chloride concentration. Cystic fibrosis is strongly suspected. Which of the following is the most appropriate quick, cost-effective first-line molecular test?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Array comparative genomic hybridization

choices.label: B
choices.text: Karyotyping of blood lymphocytes

choices.label: C
choices.text: SNP-array for common CFTR variants

choices.label: D
choices.text: Whole-exome sequencing

choices.label: E
choices.text: Whole-genome sequencing

explanation.summary: When a specific disorder with a common variant is suspected, a targeted SNP-array is the valuable, cost-effective first step.
explanation.whyCorrect: About 70% of cystic fibrosis cases are caused by the F508del mutation in CFTR (a deletion of phenylalanine at position 508). SNP-arrays detect this common mutation as a valuable first step in diagnosing diseases with common variants. Because they are less expensive than sequencing, they offer a quick and cost-effective screening method before moving on to more comprehensive analyses.

whyWrongByChoice.A: aCGH detects copy number variations, not the 3-base F508del deletion.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Karyotyping detects chromosomal abnormalities and cannot identify a small CFTR deletion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Exome sequencing is an untargeted approach reserved for when a targeted screen is negative or no candidate gene is known.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Genome sequencing is an exploratory, unbiased approach mostly used when no common mutation is suspected; it is more expensive and not the first step here.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (2 of 3), DNA analysis

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man with a 6-week cough, night sweats, and weight loss has a sputum sample sent for PCR detection of Mycobacterium tuberculosis DNA. In addition to providing a faster diagnosis than culture, the assay can detect mutations that predict resistance to which of the following drugs?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Amphotericin B and fluconazole

choices.label: B
choices.text: Azithromycin and doxycycline

choices.label: C
choices.text: Penicillin and vancomycin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Rifampicin and fluoroquinolones

choices.label: E
choices.text: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and nitrofurantoin

explanation.summary: PCR detects M. tuberculosis DNA directly and identifies mutations conferring rifampicin and fluoroquinolone resistance.
explanation.whyCorrect: M. tuberculosis DNA can be directly detected from patient samples using PCR, offering a faster diagnosis than traditional culture-based methods. PCR can also identify drug resistance by detecting mutations in genes associated with resistance to rifampicin and fluoroquinolones, helping to diagnose tuberculosis, select the most appropriate treatment, and monitor response to therapy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Amphotericin B and fluconazole are antifungal agents, not relevant to M. tuberculosis resistance testing.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Azithromycin and doxycycline are not the resistance targets of the M. tuberculosis PCR assay.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Penicillin and vancomycin are not the anti-tuberculosis drugs whose resistance mutations the PCR assay detects.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and nitrofurantoin are not tuberculosis drugs and are not assessed by this assay.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (2 of 3), DNA analysis

questions.stem: A technician prepares a PCR mixture containing template DNA, Taq polymerase, dNTPs, and forward and reverse primers in water, but forgets to add the reaction buffer. No product is obtained. Absence of which of the following buffer components most directly deprives the polymerase of a required cofactor?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Deoxyadenosine triphosphate

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dideoxynucleotides

choices.label: C
choices.text: Magnesium chloride

choices.label: D
choices.text: Potassium ions

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sodium chloride

explanation.summary: The PCR buffer supplies MgCl2, a cofactor for the DNA polymerase.
explanation.whyCorrect: The buffer creates the optimal chemical environment for enzyme activity. It regulates pH, supplies MgCl2, which is a cofactor for the polymerase, and includes potassium ions to promote primer annealing. Without magnesium the polymerase cannot function.

whyWrongByChoice.A: dATP is one of the dNTP building blocks, not a buffer component; it was already included in the mixture.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Dideoxynucleotides are chain terminators used in Sanger sequencing, not a component of the PCR buffer.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Potassium ions are in the buffer, but their role is to promote primer annealing, not to serve as the polymerase cofactor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sodium chloride is not the described polymerase cofactor; the buffer's cofactor is MgCl2.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (2 of 3), DNA analysis

questions.stem: A researcher uses an online genome database to retrieve the 5' to 3' sequence of the upper strand spanning a region of interest, and designs a forward and a reverse primer of about 20 nucleotides each. Which of the following correctly describes the reverse primer?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It anneals upstream of the target region at its 5' end

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is identical to the last ~20 bases of the upper strand at the 3' end of the target

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is identical to the ~20 bases of the upper strand immediately upstream of the target

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is the reverse-complement of the 3' end of the upper strand sequence

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is the reverse-complement of the forward primer

explanation.summary: The reverse primer is the reverse-complement of the 3' end of the 5' strand, so it matches the last bases of the 3' strand.
explanation.whyCorrect: Two primers are selected, one at the 5' (upstream) end of the target region and one downstream at the 3' end. The reverse primer has the reverse-complement sequence of the 5' strand end of the sequence, which makes it identical to the roughly 20 last bases of the 3' strand. PCR amplifies from the first nucleotide of the forward primer to the last nucleotide of the reverse primer.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The reverse primer binds downstream at the 3' end of the target; the forward primer is the one placed upstream.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The reverse primer is the complement of that stretch of the upper strand, not an identical copy; an identical copy could not anneal to it.
whyWrongByChoice.C: This describes the forward primer, which has the same sequence as the 5' strand upstream of the sequence of interest.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The two primers flank opposite ends of the target and are not complementary to each other.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (2 of 3), DNA analysis

questions.stem: After designing a new primer pair, a researcher runs a PCR and, on the agarose gel, sees several bands of different sizes instead of the single expected product. Which of the following steps in primer design was most likely neglected?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Checking primer specificity against the genome

choices.label: B
choices.text: Choosing a heat-stable polymerase

choices.label: C
choices.text: Placing one primer upstream and one downstream

choices.label: D
choices.text: Retrieving the target sequence from a genome database

choices.label: E
choices.text: Supplying MgCl2 as a polymerase cofactor

explanation.summary: Primer specificity must be checked so the primer set amplifies only the intended region and avoids off-target amplification.
explanation.whyCorrect: It is crucial to check primer specificity to ensure that the primer set amplifies only the intended region and avoids off-target amplification elsewhere in the genome. Multiple bands of different sizes indicate that the primers annealed at additional, unintended sites.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A heat-labile polymerase would be destroyed at 95 degrees C and yield no product rather than multiple bands.
whyWrongByChoice.C: If both primers were placed on the same side of the target, no product spanning the region would form; it would not generate multiple products.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Without the target sequence from a genome database, the primers could not have been designed at all; this does not explain extra bands.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Omitting the MgCl2 cofactor would abolish polymerase activity and give no product, not several products.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (2 of 3), DNA analysis

questions.stem: A laboratory sets up two separate PCRs on a thermal cycler: one amplifying a 200-bp fragment and the other a 3,000-bp fragment. The technician is told that one step of the cycle must be lengthened for the larger target. Which step is it?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Annealing at 50 to 65 degrees C

choices.label: B
choices.text: Denaturation at 95 degrees C

choices.label: C
choices.text: Elongation at 72 degrees C

choices.label: D
choices.text: Final agarose gel electrophoresis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sample collection with a swab

explanation.summary: The duration of the 72 degrees C elongation step is set according to the length of the target.
explanation.whyCorrect: During elongation at 72 degrees C, Taq polymerase extends the new strand from the bound primers. Its timing is based on target length, so a longer fragment requires a longer elongation step. Denaturation (95 degrees C, 20 to 30 seconds) and annealing (50 to 65 degrees C, 20 to 40 seconds) have fixed durations independent of product size.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Annealing at 50 to 65 degrees C lasts about 20 to 40 seconds and depends on primer binding, not product length.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Denaturation at 95 degrees C lasts about 20 to 30 seconds regardless of target length.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Gel electrophoresis is a post-PCR check, not a step of the thermal cycle.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sample collection is not a step of the PCR cycle; PCR is the molecular amplification itself, not the swab.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (2 of 3), DNA analysis

questions.stem: A single copy of a target fragment is subjected to PCR. Assuming that each cycle doubles the amount of target, approximately how many cycles are required to obtain about 1,000 copies of the fragment?

explanation.summary: PCR amplification is exponential; the final amplification ratio is 2 to the power n, where n is the number of cycles.
explanation.whyCorrect: Each PCR cycle doubles the amount of targeted region, so amplification is exponential and the final ratio is 2^n. With n = 10 cycles, 2^10 = 1,024, or roughly 1,000 copies from a single starting molecule. A full PCR usually runs 20 to 40 cycles, giving far larger yields.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 2^5 = 32 copies, far short of 1,000.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 2^20 is about one million copies, a thousand-fold more than asked.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 2^30 is about one billion copies.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 2^40 is about one trillion copies; 40 cycles is the upper end of a typical PCR run, not the answer to this calculation.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (2 of 3), DNA analysis

questions.stem: A genetics laboratory uses the enzyme DdeI to genotype a patient sample. Which of the following best describes the class of enzyme to which DdeI belongs?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A bacterial endonuclease that cuts double-stranded DNA at specific sequences

choices.label: B
choices.text: A fluorochrome-labeled dideoxynucleotide that terminates chain elongation

choices.label: C
choices.text: A heat-stable polymerase purified from Thermus aquaticus that copies DNA

choices.label: D
choices.text: A short oligonucleotide of about 20 nucleotides that flanks the target region

choices.label: E
choices.text: An exonuclease that removes nucleotides from the free end of a DNA strand

explanation.summary: Restriction enzymes are bacterial endonucleases that cut double-stranded DNA only at specific restricted sites.
explanation.whyCorrect: A restriction enzyme is a bacterial enzyme that cuts double-strand DNA at specific sequences. These enzymes are classified as endonucleases (nuclease = cuts DNA; endo = within, not at one end of the strand), so they cut DNA only at restricted sites. They are powerful tools for cloning, genome engineering, and genotyping.

whyWrongByChoice.B: This describes a ddNTP used in Sanger sequencing, not an enzyme.
whyWrongByChoice.C: This describes Taq polymerase, the enzyme that synthesizes new DNA strands in PCR.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This describes a PCR primer, not an enzyme.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Restriction enzymes are endonucleases that cut within the strand, not exonucleases acting at a free end.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (2 of 3), DNA analysis

questions.stem: A family carries a known pathogenic point mutation in a gene. Sequence analysis shows that the substitution neither creates nor abolishes any restriction enzyme recognition sequence. A relative asks to be genotyped by PCR followed by restriction enzyme digestion. Which of the following best explains why this approach is not applicable?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Point mutations can never be detected by restriction digestion

choices.label: B
choices.text: Restriction digestion cannot be performed on PCR products

choices.label: C
choices.text: Restriction enzymes cut only single-stranded DNA

choices.label: D
choices.text: RFLP genotyping requires a mutation that alters a restriction site

choices.label: E
choices.text: The mutation is novel and has no probe on any array

explanation.summary: Restriction enzyme genotyping only works for known mutations that alter a restriction site.
explanation.whyCorrect: Restriction enzyme digestion genotypes well-characterized diseases by exploiting mutations that alter a restriction enzyme recognition site. The method is only applicable to mutations that are already known and that alter a restriction site. Since this substitution leaves every recognition sequence intact, digestion would give the same pattern for mutant and wild-type alleles; sequencing would be needed instead.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Point mutations can be detected by digestion when they alter a site, as in sickle cell disease where the A-to-T change destroys the DdeI site.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Restriction digestion is routinely performed on PCR-amplified fragments; that is the standard RFLP workflow.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Restriction enzymes cut double-stranded DNA at specific sequences.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The mutation is known, not novel, and array probe content is irrelevant to whether a restriction enzyme can distinguish the alleles.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (2 of 3), DNA analysis

questions.stem: The asymptomatic parents of a child with sickle cell disease (HbSS) undergo carrier testing. A fragment of the HBB gene is amplified by PCR, digested with DdeI, and run on an agarose gel next to an undigested control of the same product. Which of the following band patterns is expected in each parent's lane?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A single band identical in size to the undigested control

choices.label: B
choices.text: A single band larger than the undigested control

choices.label: C
choices.text: No visible bands

choices.label: D
choices.text: Three bands: one undigested and two digested fragments

choices.label: E
choices.text: Two bands, both smaller than the undigested control

explanation.summary: A heterozygous carrier (HbAS) shows three bands after DdeI digestion: one uncut mutant fragment and two cut wild-type fragments.
explanation.whyCorrect: Both parents of an HbSS child are carriers (HbAS). The DdeI site is present in the normal HbA allele and lost in the HbS allele. In a heterozygote, the wild-type allele is cut into two fragments while the mutant allele remains uncut, producing three bands, one undigested and two digested fragments.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A single uncut band matching the control is the HbSS pattern, where both alleles lack the DdeI site.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Digestion cannot produce a fragment larger than the undigested product.
whyWrongByChoice.C: No bands would indicate failed PCR amplification, not a carrier genotype.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Two digested bands alone is the HbAA reference pattern, where both alleles are cut.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (2 of 3), DNA analysis

questions.stem: A PCR product is run on an agarose gel beside a DNA ladder; no restriction enzyme is used. The wild-type lane shows a single band at about 600 bp. A patient's lane shows a single band at about 300 bp, and the lane of the patient's heterozygous sibling shows two bands, at 600 bp and 300 bp. Which of the following best explains the patient's result?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Failure of PCR amplification in the patient's sample

choices.label: B
choices.text: Gain of a restriction enzyme cutting site on both alleles

choices.label: C
choices.text: Homozygous deletion of about 300 bp within the amplified region

choices.label: D
choices.text: Homozygous insertion of about 300 bp within the amplified region

choices.label: E
choices.text: Loss of a restriction enzyme cutting site on both alleles

explanation.summary: A single band smaller than wild type in an undigested PCR product indicates a homozygous deletion inside the amplification frame.
explanation.whyCorrect: If a deletion occurs inside the amplification frame defined by the primers, the PCR amplifies a smaller fragment. A single ~300 bp band in place of the 600 bp wild-type band means both alleles carry a deletion of about 300 bp (homozygous state); the heterozygous sibling shows one normal and one shortened allele.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Failed amplification would show no band at all, not a distinct 300 bp band.
whyWrongByChoice.B: No digestion was performed, and gaining a cut site would produce two fragments, not a single smaller product.
whyWrongByChoice.D: An insertion would make the homozygous band migrate higher (larger) than the wild-type band, not lower.
whyWrongByChoice.E: No restriction enzyme was used, so cutting sites are irrelevant; moreover, losing a site would leave the band uncut at full size.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (2 of 3), DNA analysis

questions.stem: In a genotyping experiment, the first well of an agarose gel is loaded with a mixture of DNA fragments of known sizes (100 bp, 200 bp, and so on up to 600 bp). What is the purpose of this lane?

choices.label: A
choices.text: To confirm that the target region was amplified at its expected size

choices.label: B
choices.text: To demonstrate the heterozygous digestion pattern

choices.label: C
choices.text: To provide size references for estimating the sample band sizes

choices.label: D
choices.text: To show the wild-type allele pattern after digestion

choices.label: E
choices.text: To verify that the restriction enzyme is active

explanation.summary: The DNA ladder lane contains fragments of known size that serve as a reference for sizing sample bands.
explanation.whyCorrect: Well 1 contains the DNA ladder, in which each band represents a known fragment size (for example 100 bp, 200 bp, up to 600 bp). Because small fragments migrate faster than large ones, comparing sample bands to the ladder allows their sizes to be estimated, such as recognizing a ~450 bp undigested PCR product.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Successful amplification is confirmed by the undigested PCR product lane showing a single band at the expected size, not by the ladder.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The heterozygous pattern (three bands) appears in the carrier's lane, not the ladder.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The wild-type digestion pattern is shown by the reference DNA lane digested with the enzyme (HbAA), which gives two bands.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Enzyme activity is demonstrated by the digested reference lane, not by the ladder.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (2 of 3), DNA analysis

questions.stem: A PCR product from a patient suspected of carrying an uncharacterized CFTR mutation is run on an agarose gel and shows a single band at the expected size. The referring physician asks whether the patient's mutation has now been identified. Which of the following is the most accurate response?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No; electrophoresis confirms amplification but does not reveal the DNA sequence

choices.label: B
choices.text: No; the band should be hybridized to a SNP-array to read its sequence

choices.label: C
choices.text: No; the product must first be digested with DdeI to identify the mutation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes; a band at the expected size excludes any pathogenic variant

choices.label: E
choices.text: Yes; a single band indicates a homozygous wild-type genotype

explanation.summary: Gel electrophoresis is a preliminary check of PCR success; it does not reveal the exact DNA sequence.
explanation.whyCorrect: Electrophoresis is a fast and inexpensive method to confirm whether PCR successfully amplified the target and to analyze restriction digestion patterns for genotyping. It is often used as a preliminary check before sequencing the PCR product, but it does not reveal the exact DNA sequence. The amplified product must now be sequenced.

whyWrongByChoice.B: SNP-arrays do not read sequence and only detect variants with probes on the chip; an uncharacterized mutation would be missed.
whyWrongByChoice.C: DdeI digestion genotypes the known sickle cell HBB mutation; it is not a general method for identifying an unknown CFTR variant.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A correctly sized band only shows amplification worked; a point mutation does not change fragment size.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A single band of expected size gives no genotype information without digestion or sequencing.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (2 of 3), DNA analysis

questions.stem: A student who has just completed a PCR now prepares a Sanger sequencing reaction on the purified product and asks how the reagent list differs. Which of the following correctly distinguishes the Sanger reaction mixture from that of PCR?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Sanger sequencing needs no DNA polymerase, since the primer extends on its own

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sanger sequencing needs no template, since the ddNTPs assemble the strand

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sanger sequencing omits deoxynucleotides entirely and uses only terminators

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sanger sequencing uses a single primer rather than a forward and reverse pair

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sanger sequencing uses unlabeled nucleotides rather than fluorochromes

explanation.summary: Sanger sequencing uses one primer to define the starting point of synthesis, whereas PCR uses two flanking primers.
explanation.whyCorrect: The sequencing reaction requires the DNA sample (PCR product), a DNA polymerase, dNTPs, and one primer to define the starting point of synthesis, because DNA polymerase needs a double-stranded region, provided by the primer binding the template, to initiate synthesis. Lastly, fluorochrome-labeled ddNTPs are added. PCR, by contrast, requires two primers (forward and reverse) that flank and define the fragment to be amplified.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Sanger sequencing requires a DNA polymerase to synthesize the complementary strand.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The PCR product serves as the template DNA sample for the sequencing reaction.
whyWrongByChoice.C: dNTPs are required; ddNTPs are added in addition, at much lower concentration.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The ddNTPs are labeled with fluorochromes so the terminal base of each fragment can be detected.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (2 of 3), DNA analysis

questions.stem: In a Sanger sequencing run, the polymerase reaction has produced a collection of fluorescently labeled DNA fragments of varying lengths, each ending with a labeled base. Which of the following steps allows the original sequence to be read from these fragments?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Alignment of millions of short reads to a reference genome

choices.label: B
choices.text: Capillary electrophoresis with laser detection of each fragment's terminal base

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fragmentation of the labeled products and ligation of sequencing adapters

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hybridization of the labeled fragments to allele-specific probes on a chip

choices.label: E
choices.text: Restriction enzyme digestion of the fragments followed by agarose gel electrophoresis

explanation.summary: Capillary electrophoresis separates the Sanger fragments by size and a laser detects the labeled terminal base of each.
explanation.whyCorrect: Capillary electrophoresis separates the fragments by size and detects them using a laser. Because each fragment ends with the base specified by its fluorescently labeled ddNTP, reading the labels in order of fragment length reconstructs the sequence by reading the complementary bases in order. The result is displayed as an electropherogram in which each peak represents a single nucleotide.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aligning millions of reads is the bioinformatic step of NGS, which processes millions of fragments simultaneously.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fragmentation and adapter ligation are the library-preparation steps of next-generation sequencing, not Sanger sequencing.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Chip hybridization is the SNP-array approach and does not read a sequence base by base.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Restriction digestion is a genotyping method for known site-altering mutations; it does not read the terminal base of sequencing fragments.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (2 of 3), DNA analysis

questions.stem: A Sanger electropherogram of a patient's gene shows clean, single peaks for the first 120 bases. From base 121 onward, two overlapping sequences are seen at every position through the end of the read. Which of the following is the most likely interpretation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A heterozygous insertion or deletion beginning near position 121

choices.label: B
choices.text: A heterozygous point mutation affecting only position 121

choices.label: C
choices.text: A homozygous deletion of bases beginning near position 121

choices.label: D
choices.text: A homozygous point mutation affecting only position 121

choices.label: E
choices.text: Failure of the sequencing reaction beyond position 120

explanation.summary: Overlapping sequences from a specific point onward indicate a heterozygous indel that shifts the alignment of the two alleles.
explanation.whyCorrect: Overlapping sequences from a specific point typically indicate an insertion or deletion (indel), where the sequence alignment shows a shift starting at a particular position due to added or missing bases on one allele. Sanger sequencing detects point mutations and small indels in selected regions, and overlapping peaks reflect a mixed signal as seen in heterozygous individuals.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A heterozygous point mutation gives two overlapping peaks at a single position only, with clean peaks afterward.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A homozygous deletion would give a single clean sequence simply missing the deleted bases; overlap requires two different alleles.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A homozygous point mutation produces a single clean peak of a different base at one position, with no overlap.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A failed reaction would yield no readable peaks, not two interpretable overlapping sequences.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (2 of 3), DNA analysis

questions.stem: A laboratory prepares a patient's DNA for whole-exome sequencing on a next-generation sequencing platform. Which of the following is the correct sequence of steps in this workflow?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Annealing of a single primer, random ddNTP incorporation, capillary electrophoresis, laser detection

choices.label: B
choices.text: Denaturation at 95 degrees C, primer annealing, elongation at 72 degrees C, repeated for 20 to 40 cycles

choices.label: C
choices.text: DNA fragmentation, adapter ligation to create a library, PCR amplification, base-by-base reading of the library fragments

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hybridization of labeled DNA to probes on a chip, fluorescence scanning, allele-specific dosage plots

choices.label: E
choices.text: Restriction enzyme digestion, agarose gel electrophoresis, comparison of band sizes to a DNA ladder

explanation.summary: NGS begins with DNA fragmentation and adapter addition to build a library, followed by amplification and base-by-base reading.
explanation.whyCorrect: NGS begins with the fragmentation of DNA, followed by the addition of adapters to create a sequencing library. These fragments are then amplified (PCR) and loaded onto a sequencing platform where they are read base by base, using methods such as sequencing by synthesis to detect nucleotide incorporation. Millions of fragments are processed simultaneously, and bioinformatic analysis aligns the reads and identifies mutations.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This is the Sanger sequencing workflow, which reads one selected region rather than millions of fragments at once.
whyWrongByChoice.B: This is the PCR thermal cycle used to amplify a specific segment; it is one component of library preparation, not the whole NGS workflow.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This is the SNP-microarray workflow, a targeted genotyping panel rather than sequencing.
whyWrongByChoice.E: This is the RFLP genotyping workflow, which detects only known site-altering mutations.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (2 of 3), DNA analysis

questions.stem: Whole-exome sequencing of a child with an undiagnosed disorder identifies about 35,000 variants relative to the reference human genome, delivered as a FASTQ file and summarized by bioinformaticians. Which of the following filtering steps is typically applied first to narrow this list to candidate variants?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Assessing conservation of each variant across species

choices.label: B
choices.text: Classifying variants as missense, nonsense, or frameshift

choices.label: C
choices.text: Excluding common variants found in population databases

choices.label: D
choices.text: Prioritizing variants in genes already associated with the phenotype

choices.label: E
choices.text: Restricting to variants consistent with a recessive inheritance pattern

explanation.summary: Variant filtering begins by excluding common population variants to focus on rare or novel ones.
explanation.whyCorrect: Typical exome sequencing identifies between 20,000 and 50,000 variants compared to a reference genome. These undergo a multi-step filtering process: initially, common variants found in population databases are excluded to focus on rare or novel ones. Next, variants are filtered by predicted impact (missense, nonsense, frameshift), then assessed for location in genes associated with the phenotype, with additional filters for inheritance pattern and conservation across species.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Conservation across species is one of the additional, later filters, not the initial step.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Filtering by predicted impact is the second step, applied after common variants are removed.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Assessing location in phenotype-associated genes comes after the common-variant and impact filters.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Inheritance-pattern filtering (dominant, recessive) is an additional later filter.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (2 of 3), DNA analysis

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman has progressive numbness, weakness, difficulty walking, and vision changes from an autoimmune attack on the myelin sheath. Investigators studying patients with this disease perform whole-exome sequencing on ten patients with benign disease and ten with aggressive disease, rather than a targeted SNP-array. Which of the following characteristics of the disease best justifies the unbiased exome approach?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is a multi-locus disease with no single candidate gene

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is caused by expansion of a trinucleotide repeat

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is caused by one common point mutation in a known gene

choices.label: D
choices.text: It results from a balanced translocation between two chromosomes

choices.label: E
choices.text: It results from copy-number loss detectable by aCGH

explanation.summary: When the phenotype-genotype correlation is unclear and no candidate locus exists, an unbiased approach such as exome sequencing is used.
explanation.whyCorrect: Multiple sclerosis is a progressive autoimmune, multifactorial disease in which the correlation between phenotype and genotype remains unclear, as in many multi-locus genetic diseases. With no specific candidate gene or locus in mind, an unbiased approach is appropriate. Gil-Varea et al. performed WES on ten benign and ten aggressive patients, screened sixteen SNPs in larger cohorts, and found that mutations in CPXM2, IGSF9B, and NLRP9 are associated with the aggressive form and may serve as biomarkers of progression.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Repeat expansions are poorly detected by NGS and are not the basis of this disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A highly suspected disorder with a single common mutation would call for a targeted approach such as a SNP-array, not exome sequencing.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Balanced translocations are often missed by NGS and are not the basis of this disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Copy-number loss would be investigated with aCGH or a SNP-array, not exome sequencing, and is not the basis of this disease.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (2 of 3), DNA analysis

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man has a progressive neurologic disorder with a family history consistent with a condition known to be caused by expansion of a DNA repeat. Whole-exome sequencing by NGS returns no pathogenic variant. Which of the following best explains this negative result?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Exome sequencing cannot detect small indels

choices.label: B
choices.text: NGS has poor capability for detecting repeat expansions

choices.label: C
choices.text: NGS has poor sensitivity for single-nucleotide variants

choices.label: D
choices.text: Repeat expansions are detected only by SNP-array

choices.label: E
choices.text: The sequencing depth used was too high for this variant

explanation.summary: NGS detects SNVs and small indels well but performs poorly for repeat expansions.
explanation.whyCorrect: NGS detection capability varies by mutation type: SNVs are detected excellently and small indels well, CNVs variably depending on size, structural variants moderately, low-level mosaicism only with high depth, while repeat expansions are detected poorly, epigenetic changes are not detected directly, and balanced translocations are often missed.
