whyWrongByChoice.E: Endosomal escape concerns delivery of synthetic siRNA into the cytoplasm, not mutation discovery.

questions.topicName: From Bench to Bedside: The Role of Animal Models in Novel Therapeutics

questions.stem: Rather than inducing mutations, a pharmacology group applies a library of FDA-approved compounds to cultured cardiomyocytes and uses automated assays of electrophysiology, contractility, calcium handling, and cell viability. Which benefit does this phenotypic screening approach provide?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It finds new uses for existing drugs, bypassing early development

choices.label: B
choices.text: It permanently corrects mutations in the screened cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: It produces heritable models that can be bred to homozygosity

choices.label: D
choices.text: It removes the FDA requirement for preclinical safety studies

choices.label: E
choices.text: It silences overexpressed genes in the treated cells

explanation.summary: High-throughput phenotypic screens of approved drugs accelerate repurposing and toxicity prediction.
explanation.whyCorrect: Phenotypic selection remains widely used in pre-clinical research, especially in drug screening: instead of inducing mutations, researchers observe how compounds affect cellular functions. High-throughput screens of FDA-approved drug libraries on cardiomyocytes accelerate drug repurposing by identifying new applications for existing compounds, bypassing early development phases, and improve human-relevant cardiotoxicity prediction.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Applying compounds to cells does not alter their DNA sequence or correct any mutation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cultured cardiomyocytes are not bred; heritable lines come from genetically modified animals.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Preclinical animal studies of safety and efficacy before human trials are mandated by the FDA and are not waived.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Silencing overexpressed genes is a function of RNA interference, not of a compound screen.

questions.topicName: From Bench to Bedside: The Role of Animal Models in Novel Therapeutics

questions.stem: Embryonic stem cells carrying a disrupted gene are selected with a resistance marker and injected into blastocysts, and the resulting mice carry the mutation in only some of their cells. Why must these animals be bred before a heterozygous line can be established?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Because heterozygotes arise only when the germ cells contain the knock-out allele

choices.label: B
choices.text: Because homozygous animals must be obtained before heterozygotes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Because the disrupted gene is silenced in all somatic tissues

choices.label: D
choices.text: Because the injected stem cells are lost during gestation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Because the resistance cassette must be removed before breeding

explanation.summary: Chimeric founders transmit the mutation only if their germ cells carry it.
explanation.whyCorrect: Knock-out embryonic stem cells selected with the resistance marker are injected into blastocysts, producing chimeric mice in which only some cells carry the mutation, a mosaicism. Breeding these chimeras generates heterozygotes when the germ cells carry the mutation, and homozygous animals can be obtained later.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The order is the reverse: heterozygotes are obtained first, and homozygotes are bred from them afterwards.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The mutation is a physical disruption of the DNA sequence, not a reversible silencing of the gene.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The injected cells contribute to the chimeric animal's tissues; the issue is which tissues they populate.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The neomycin-resistance cassette disrupts the gene and is what makes the allele null; it is not removed to allow breeding.

questions.topicName: From Bench to Bedside: The Role of Animal Models in Novel Therapeutics

questions.stem: Sequencing a bacterial chromosome reveals clusters of short repeated sequences of about 23 to 55 base pairs, separated by unique segments whose sequences match DNA from bacteriophages the strain has previously encountered. What is the function of these unique segments?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They encode the nuclease that cuts the invading DNA

choices.label: B
choices.text: They form the scaffold that binds the nuclease

choices.label: C
choices.text: They mark the site three base pairs from each cut

choices.label: D
choices.text: They provide a molecular memory of prior viral infection

choices.label: E
choices.text: They shield the bacterial chromosome from its own nuclease

explanation.summary: CRISPR spacers are stored viral sequences that serve as immunologic memory.
explanation.whyCorrect: CRISPR arrays are clusters of short, repetitive DNA sequences within the bacterial chromosome, with repeats of roughly 23 to 55 base pairs. Between the repeats lie spacers, fragments of viral DNA acquired during previous infections, which serve as a molecular memory allowing the bacterium to recognize and defend against recurring viral threats.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The nuclease is encoded by the separate Cas genes adjacent to the array, not by the spacers themselves.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The scaffold that binds Cas9 is the constant region of the guide RNA, derived from tracrRNA.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The cut position three base pairs upstream is specified by the PAM in the target DNA, not by a spacer.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Spacers record foreign sequences; they do not act as a shield over the bacterial genome.

questions.topicName: From Bench to Bedside: The Role of Animal Models in Novel Therapeutics

questions.stem: Cas proteins encoded next to CRISPR arrays all belong to a single enzymatic class, of which Cas9 is the member most widely used in biotechnology. What type of enzyme are they?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Helicases that unwind the double helix

choices.label: B
choices.text: Kinases that phosphorylate target proteins

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ligases that join DNA ends together

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nucleases that cut or degrade nucleic acids

choices.label: E
choices.text: Polymerases that synthesize new DNA strands

explanation.summary: Cas proteins are nucleases; Cas9 is the one most used in biotechnology.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cas proteins are nucleases, enzymes that cut or degrade nucleic acids. Several types exist with specific roles in bacterial immunity and genetic research, and Cas9 is the most widely used in biotechnology because it can be programmed to target and cut specific DNA sequences with high precision.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Unwinding of the helix is not the defining catalytic activity of this family.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cas proteins act on nucleic acids rather than phosphorylating proteins.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Joining DNA ends is performed by the cell's own repair machinery after Cas9 has cut.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Synthesis of new DNA strands is not the activity attributed to Cas proteins.

questions.topicName: From Bench to Bedside: The Role of Animal Models in Novel Therapeutics

questions.stem: Two scientists described the CRISPR-Cas9 system as a programmable gene-editing tool in 2012 and were later recognized with a Nobel Prize. Which prize did Emmanuelle Charpentier and Jennifer Doudna receive?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2006

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2020

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 2006

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 2012

choices.label: E
choices.text: The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 2020

explanation.summary: Charpentier and Doudna won the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for CRISPR-Cas9.
explanation.whyCorrect: In 2012 Emmanuelle Charpentier and Jennifer Doudna described the CRISPR-Cas9 system, and these French and American scientists were awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2020. Cas9 functions as molecular scissors for gene editing in bacteria and in eukaryotic cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 2006 is the wrong year, and the 2006 prize relevant to this material was not in Chemistry.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The 2006 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine went to Fire and Mello for the discovery of RNA interference.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 2012 is the year the system was described, not the year a prize was awarded.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The prize awarded for this work was in Chemistry rather than Physiology or Medicine.

questions.topicName: From Bench to Bedside: The Role of Animal Models in Novel Therapeutics

questions.stem: A guide RNA is built with a 20-nucleotide variable region that is perfectly complementary to a sequence found only once in the target gene, yet Cas9 repeatedly fails to cut at that site. Which design requirement has most likely not been met?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The break must be repaired by homologous recombination

choices.label: B
choices.text: The constant region must be unique to each experiment

choices.label: C
choices.text: The guide RNA must be supplied as two separate molecules

choices.label: D
choices.text: The target site must lie immediately upstream of a PAM

choices.label: E
choices.text: The variable region must be at least 50 nucleotides long

explanation.summary: A spacer only works if its target sits immediately upstream of a PAM sequence.
explanation.whyCorrect: The variable region, or spacer, is a 20-nucleotide sequence unique to each experiment that must be unique in the genome to avoid off-target effects and must be located immediately upstream of a PAM sequence. Cas9 cuts three base pairs upstream of the PAM, so without an adjacent PAM no cut occurs even with perfect complementarity.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Repair pathway choice determines the outcome after cutting and cannot explain a failure to cut at all.
whyWrongByChoice.B: It is the variable region that is unique to each experiment; the constant scaffold region is the same across all guide RNAs.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A single guide RNA fuses the two RNA components into one molecule, as originally described.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The spacer is specified as 20 nucleotides; a much longer variable region is not a requirement.

questions.topicName: From Bench to Bedside: The Role of Animal Models in Novel Therapeutics

questions.stem: A laboratory planning a CRISPR-Cas9 experiment in mouse embryos has assembled the Cas9 protein and the guide RNA and must now introduce both into the cells. Which set of methods is used for this purpose?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Breeding of chimeric animals to homozygosity

choices.label: B
choices.text: Chemical mutagenesis of the fertilized egg

choices.label: C
choices.text: Endocytosis followed by endosomal escape alone

choices.label: D
choices.text: Microinjection, electroporation, or viral delivery

choices.label: E
choices.text: Selection with a neomycin-resistance cassette

explanation.summary: Cas9 and guide RNA are delivered by microinjection, electroporation, or viral systems.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cas9 protein, guide RNA, and the genomic DNA target are necessary and sufficient for CRISPR-Cas9 to cut DNA. In a typical genome-editing experiment the Cas9 protein and guide RNA are introduced into cells or organisms via microinjection, electroporation, or viral delivery systems.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Breeding propagates an edit that already exists rather than introducing the components.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Chemical mutagenesis creates random mutations and delivers nothing to the cell.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Endocytosis and endosomal escape describe how synthetic siRNA reaches the cytoplasm, not how editing components are introduced here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A resistance cassette is used to select cells after homologous recombination, not to deliver the editing components.

questions.topicName: From Bench to Bedside: The Role of Animal Models in Novel Therapeutics

questions.stem: A patient with sickle cell disease receives the first CRISPR-Cas9 therapy approved by the FDA. Blood stem cells are withdrawn from the bone marrow and edited outside the body, the patient is then conditioned by irradiation to remove the remaining marrow cells, and the edited cells are implanted back. Which description best characterizes this treatment strategy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Allele-specific silencing at the messenger RNA level

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ex vivo somatic editing of the patient's own stem cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Germline editing of the patient's future offspring

choices.label: D
choices.text: In vivo somatic editing by injected Cas9 and guide RNA

choices.label: E
choices.text: Random mutagenesis followed by phenotypic selection

explanation.summary: Casgevy is an ex vivo somatic editing therapy for sickle cell disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: Casgevy, the first CRISPR-Cas9 based therapy approved by the FDA, treats or even cures sickle cell disease using an ex vivo editing strategy. Blood stem cells are extracted from the patient's bone marrow and edited with CRISPR-Cas9, the patient is conditioned to remove remaining marrow cells, and the edited stem cells are implanted back so that new cells produce functional hemoglobin.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Silencing at the mRNA level describes siRNA therapy, whereas this approach edits the DNA of the cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Editing blood stem cells is somatic and does not affect future generations; germline editing is banned or highly regulated in most countries.
whyWrongByChoice.D: In vivo editing would require injecting the Cas9 ribonucleoprotein into the patient, which the described workflow avoids by editing outside the body.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Random mutagenesis is an untargeted research technique and is not a therapeutic strategy.

questions.topicName: From Bench to Bedside: The Role of Animal Models in Novel Therapeutics

questions.stem: In 2018 a scientist used CRISPR to edit human embryos, intending to reproduce a naturally occurring deletion that makes carriers resistant to HIV infection by altering a protein on the surface of immune cells that the virus uses to enter them. Which gene was targeted?

choices.label: A
choices.text: APP

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cas9

choices.label: C
choices.text: CCR5

choices.label: D
choices.text: HTT

choices.label: E
choices.text: krtt1c19e

explanation.summary: He Jiankui targeted CCR5, attempting to recreate the CCR5-delta32 variant.
explanation.whyCorrect: In 2018 He Jiankui used CRISPR to edit embryos, producing genetically modified babies. He targeted the CCR5 gene, which encodes a protein on the surface of immune cells used as a doorway by HIV to enter and infect them, intending to replicate the natural CCR5-delta32 mutation. He did not reproduce that specific mutation, the process led to mosaicism, and many countries subsequently tightened regulation of gene editing.

whyWrongByChoice.A: APP produces the beta-amyloid plaques of Alzheimer disease and is a proposed siRNA target.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cas9 is the bacterial nuclease used as the editing tool rather than the gene being edited.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HTT is the huntingtin gene targeted by allele-specific siRNA strategies in Huntington disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: krtt1c19e encodes keratin 19 and is tagged with a fluorescent protein to visualize epithelial cells.

questions.topicName: From Bench to Bedside: The Role of Animal Models in Novel Therapeutics

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman whose first pregnancy was affected by an open neural tube defect asks about the chance that a future pregnancy will be similarly affected. Neither she nor her partner has any known family history of the condition. Which of the following best estimates this risk and the concept it illustrates?

choices.label: A
choices.text: About 25%, reflecting autosomal recessive inheritance

choices.label: B
choices.text: About 50%, reflecting autosomal dominant inheritance

choices.label: C
choices.text: Approximately 1 in 1,500, equal to the general-population occurrence risk

choices.label: D
choices.text: Approximately 2-5%, reflecting recurrence risk in a multifactorial disorder

choices.label: E
choices.text: Essentially 0%, because neural tube defects are purely environmental

explanation.summary: Recurrence risk is the chance of disease when a family member is already affected, and for neural tube defects it is roughly 2-5%.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that women who have had a child with a neural tube defect face a recurrence risk of approximately 2-5% in future pregnancies, about 37.5 times higher than the general-population occurrence risk of ~1 in 1,500. Multifactorial disorders do not follow Mendelian fractions.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A 25% risk implies autosomal recessive single-gene inheritance, which does not describe multifactorial neural tube defects.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A 50% risk implies autosomal dominant single-gene inheritance, which does not apply here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 1 in 1,500 is the general-population occurrence risk, not the recurrence risk after an affected child.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Neural tube defects are multifactorial, with both genetic and environmental contributions, so recurrence risk is elevated, not zero.

questions.topicName: Multifactorial Disorders

questions.stem: A healthy 40-year-old man with no relatives affected by Alzheimer disease asks his physician, "What is my chance of ever developing Alzheimer disease?" This question is best described by which of the following terms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Complete penetrance

choices.label: B
choices.text: Concordance rate

choices.label: C
choices.text: Occurrence risk

choices.label: D
choices.text: Recurrence risk

choices.label: E
choices.text: Relative risk reduction

explanation.summary: Occurrence risk is the chance of being affected by a disease without a family history of it.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines occurrence risk as the chance of being affected by a disease when no one in the family has had it, using the example of Alzheimer disease with no affected relatives. Because this man has no family history, his question concerns occurrence risk.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Penetrance describes the proportion of genotype carriers who express the phenotype, not this risk question.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Concordance rate is a twin-study measure of whether both twins share a disease, not an individual's baseline risk.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Recurrence risk applies when a family member is already affected, which is not the case here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Relative risk reduction is a treatment-effect measure, unrelated to baseline disease risk.

questions.topicName: Multifactorial Disorders

questions.stem: In the liability-threshold model of multifactorial disease, a particular condition has a very high threshold. Which of the following is most likely true of this condition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It affects males and females at exactly equal rates

choices.label: B
choices.text: It follows a single-gene, autosomal dominant inheritance pattern

choices.label: C
choices.text: It has a high prevalence in the general population

choices.label: D
choices.text: It has a low prevalence in the general population

choices.label: E
choices.text: Recurrence risk is independent of how many relatives are affected

explanation.summary: A higher threshold means fewer people cross it (lower prevalence) but affected individuals carry more risk factors, raising familial recurrence risk.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick teaches that the higher the threshold, the lower the population prevalence, because a greater combined genetic and environmental load is required to become affected. It also states that a higher threshold means a higher recurrence risk within families, because affected individuals likely carry more genetic risk factors that relatives may share.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Thresholds and prevalence can differ between sexes; equal rates are not implied by a high threshold.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Multifactorial disorders do not follow single-gene Mendelian inheritance patterns.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A high threshold lowers, not raises, population prevalence.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Recurrence risk rises with more affected relatives and a heavier genetic load, so it is not independent of family involvement.

questions.topicName: Multifactorial Disorders

questions.stem: Pyloric stenosis is roughly four times more common in male than in female infants. A female infant is diagnosed with pyloric stenosis. Based on the liability-threshold model, which of the following best describes the implication for her future siblings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Because an affected female must exceed a higher threshold, she likely carries a greater genetic load

choices.label: B
choices.text: Because females have a lower liability threshold, her siblings carry a below-average risk of disease

choices.label: C
choices.text: Her siblings have no increased risk because pyloric stenosis is purely environmental in origin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Only her sisters, and not her brothers, are at increased risk of developing pyloric stenosis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Recurrence risk is 50% for each sibling, consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance

explanation.summary: When the less-often-affected sex is affected, that individual carries a heavier genetic load, increasing recurrence risk in relatives.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that females have a higher threshold for pyloric stenosis, so an affected female must carry a greater genetic and environmental load. As a result her relatives are significantly more likely to inherit these risk factors, producing a higher recurrence risk within the family.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Females have a higher, not lower, threshold for pyloric stenosis, so this reasoning is reversed.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pyloric stenosis is multifactorial with a strong genetic contribution, not purely environmental.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Both brothers and sisters can inherit the shared genetic risk factors; risk is not limited to sisters.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A fixed 50% recurrence reflects autosomal dominant single-gene inheritance, which does not apply to this multifactorial condition.

questions.topicName: Multifactorial Disorders

questions.stem: Monozygotic twins share nearly identical genomes. For a particular disease, researchers observe that many monozygotic twin pairs are discordant, meaning only one twin of the pair is affected. This discordance most strongly indicates which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Non-genetic factors contribute to the disease

choices.label: B
choices.text: The disease cannot be inherited at all

choices.label: C
choices.text: The disease has complete penetrance

choices.label: D
choices.text: The disease is caused by a single dominant gene

choices.label: E
choices.text: The twins must actually be dizygotic

explanation.summary: Discordance in genetically identical twins points to a non-genetic (multifactorial) contribution.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that because monozygotic twins have nearly identical genotypes, the existence of discordant pairs (only one affected) indicates that non-genetic factors contribute to the disease, supporting a multifactorial origin.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Discordance shows environmental influence but does not mean the disease has no heritable component.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Complete penetrance would produce concordance in identical twins, the opposite of what is observed.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A single dominant gene would tend to make identical twins concordant, not discordant.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The premise states the twins are monozygotic; discordance does not change their zygosity.

questions.topicName: Multifactorial Disorders

questions.stem: A twin study reports the concordance rate for oral clefts as 50% in monozygotic twins and 8% in dizygotic twins. Which of the following conclusions is best supported by these data?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dizygotic twins should always be concordant for oral cleft

choices.label: B
choices.text: Genetic factors are unimportant because monozygotic concordance is only 50%

choices.label: C
choices.text: Oral cleft has no genetic contribution

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oral cleft is a single-gene disorder with complete penetrance

choices.label: E
choices.text: Oral cleft is multifactorial with a substantial genetic component

explanation.summary: Higher concordance in monozygotic than dizygotic twins, with MZ concordance well below 100%, indicates a multifactorial disease with a strong genetic component.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick uses this exact example: because concordance is higher in monozygotic (50%) than dizygotic (8%) twins, oral cleft has a strong genetic component; because 50% of monozygotic pairs are still discordant, it is classified as multifactorial rather than purely genetic.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Dizygotic twins share only about half their genes on average, so they are not expected to be always concordant.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The higher monozygotic concordance actually signals that genetics is important; 50% simply also implicates environment.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The much higher monozygotic than dizygotic concordance demonstrates a clear genetic contribution.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A single-gene, fully penetrant disorder would produce near-100% monozygotic concordance, not 50%.

questions.topicName: Multifactorial Disorders

questions.stem: A research team scans the genomes of 20,000 individuals with ADHD and 35,000 unaffected controls to identify single-nucleotide polymorphisms that occur more frequently in affected individuals, then displays the results as a Manhattan plot. This approach is best described as which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A genome-wide association study (GWAS)

choices.label: B
choices.text: A randomized controlled trial

choices.label: C
choices.text: A twin study

choices.label: D
choices.text: Karyotype analysis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Linkage analysis within a single large family

explanation.summary: GWAS scans many genomes to find SNPs that are more common in affected than unaffected people.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines GWAS as scanning the genomes of thousands to millions of individuals to find SNPs that occur more frequently in people with a disease than in those without it, and it describes an ADHD meta-analysis of 20,183 cases and 35,191 controls visualized with a Manhattan plot.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A randomized controlled trial tests interventions, not inherent genetic associations.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Twin studies compare disease concordance in twin pairs; they do not scan genome-wide SNP frequencies across large case-control cohorts.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Karyotyping examines chromosome number and structure, not individual SNP associations.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Linkage analysis tracks markers co-segregating with disease in families, not population-level SNP frequency comparisons.

questions.topicName: Multifactorial Disorders

questions.stem: In population genetics, DNA sequence variants are classified by how often they occur. A benign variant present in more than 1% of the population is best classified as which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A de novo pathogenic variant

choices.label: B
choices.text: A deleterious mutation

choices.label: C
choices.text: A frameshift mutation

choices.label: D
choices.text: A polymorphism

choices.label: E
choices.text: Aneuploidy

explanation.summary: Polymorphisms are benign variants with a population frequency greater than 1%.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines polymorphisms as benign mutations with a frequency greater than 1%, noting that a human genome typically carries 5-10 million single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs). Some of these common SNPs are now recognized as disease risk factors.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A de novo pathogenic variant is a new, typically rare, disease-causing change, not a common benign one.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Deleterious mutations are rare variants with a direct disease-causing effect, not benign high-frequency variants.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A frameshift mutation is a specific disruptive coding change, not a frequency-based classification.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Aneuploidy is an abnormal chromosome number, a different category of variation.

questions.topicName: Multifactorial Disorders

questions.stem: A patient is started on warfarin, which has a narrow therapeutic window. Genetic testing reveals a CYP2C9 variant that reduces the activity of the hepatic enzyme that metabolizes the drug. Which of the following is the most appropriate expectation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The patient will accumulate higher warfarin levels and require a lower dose

choices.label: B
choices.text: The patient will clear warfarin faster and require a higher dose

choices.label: C
choices.text: The variant acts by directly increasing vitamin K epoxide reductase expression

choices.label: D
choices.text: The variant eliminates any need for INR monitoring

choices.label: E
choices.text: Warfarin will be ineffective regardless of the dose used

explanation.summary: Reduced CYP2C9 activity slows warfarin breakdown, raising drug levels so a lower dose is needed to avoid bleeding.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that CYP2C9 encodes the liver enzyme that breaks down warfarin, and certain variants slow this process, increasing drug levels in the blood. Patients with such variants may therefore require lower doses to avoid bleeding, and this pharmacogenomic information is used to personalize dosing.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Reduced enzyme activity slows clearance, so the drug accumulates and a lower, not higher, dose is needed.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Altering vitamin K epoxide reductase expression is the mechanism of VKORC1 variants, not CYP2C9.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Warfarin still requires INR monitoring; pharmacogenomic testing complements, not replaces, it.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Warfarin remains effective; the concern is excess drug levels, not loss of effect.

questions.topicName: Multifactorial Disorders

questions.stem: Genome-wide association studies of migraine identified risk loci containing the CALCA and CALCB genes, which encode calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP). This finding helps explain the effectiveness of which class of migraine therapy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anti-CGRP monoclonal antibodies and gepants

choices.label: B
choices.text: Broad-spectrum antibiotics such as doxycycline

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inhaled corticosteroids such as budesonide

choices.label: D
choices.text: Proton pump inhibitors such as omeprazole

choices.label: E
choices.text: Warfarin and other vitamin K antagonist anticoagulants

explanation.summary: CALCA/CALCB encode CGRP, the target of anti-CGRP monoclonal antibodies and gepants.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick notes that newly identified migraine risk loci include genes encoding migraine-specific drug targets, specifically CGRP (CALCA/CALCB), which is the target of preventive and acute therapies delivered as monoclonal antibodies and gepants.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Antibiotics treat infections and have no role in the CGRP pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Inhaled corticosteroids treat airway inflammation, not CGRP-mediated migraine.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Proton pump inhibitors reduce gastric acid and are not migraine-specific CGRP agents.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vitamin K antagonists are anticoagulants, unrelated to CGRP-directed migraine therapy.

questions.topicName: Multifactorial Disorders

questions.stem: Studies suggest that a grandmother's smoking during pregnancy may alter DNA methylation patterns that are detectable in her daughter and potentially in her grandchildren. This phenomenon is best termed which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Classic Mendelian inheritance

choices.label: B
choices.text: Genetic anticipation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Genomic imprinting limited to a single generation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Somatic mosaicism

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transgenerational epigenetic inheritance

explanation.summary: Prenatal exposures altering methylation across multiple generations is transgenerational epigenetic inheritance.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes how a grandmother's smoking during pregnancy may alter DNA methylation in her daughter and potentially her grandchildren, and names this phenomenon transgenerational epigenetic inheritance, in which prenatal environmental exposures influence outcomes beyond the immediate generation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Mendelian inheritance involves transmission of DNA-sequence alleles, whereas this involves epigenetic marks.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Anticipation is worsening or earlier disease onset over generations (as in trinucleotide repeat disorders), not methylation changes from an ancestor's exposure.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Genomic imprinting involves parent-of-origin gene silencing, not smoking-induced effects transmitted across several generations.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Somatic mosaicism refers to genetically different cell populations within one individual, not inherited methylation changes.

questions.topicName: Multifactorial Disorders

questions.stem: A medical student explains to a patient that allelic variation underlies much of human phenotypic diversity. Which of the following statements best describes the role of allelic variation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It affects only single-gene Mendelian disorders and no other human traits

choices.label: B
choices.text: It contributes only to disease and never to normal inherited human traits

choices.label: C
choices.text: It contributes to normal traits as well as to disease susceptibility

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is largely irrelevant to human genetics and phenotypic diversity

choices.label: E
choices.text: It occurs only within the non-coding regions of the human genome

explanation.summary: Allelic variation shapes both normal phenotypic traits and susceptibility to disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick teaches that allelic variation contributes to normal traits, disease susceptibility, and disease itself, giving examples such as body size (multifactorial) and eye color (multigenic), and states that these variants occur in both coding and non-coding regions of DNA.

whyWrongByChoice.A: It contributes to multifactorial and multigenic traits, not just single-gene Mendelian disorders.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Allelic variation affects normal traits like size and eye color, not disease alone.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Allelic variation is central to human genetic and phenotypic diversity, not irrelevant.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Variation occurs in both coding and non-coding regions, not only non-coding DNA.

questions.topicName: Multifactorial Disorders

questions.stem: A physician has practiced for decades in a small, historically isolated town whose residents were once nearly all descendants of southern European immigrants. Over the past two generations, young adults have left to study elsewhere, married partners of diverse backgrounds, and returned to raise families, so the town is now genetically mixed. The physician notices that the incidence of thalassemia minor has steadily declined. Which population-genetics concept best explains this observation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Assortative mating

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bottleneck effect

choices.label: C
choices.text: Founder effect

choices.label: D
choices.text: Gene flow

choices.label: E
choices.text: Genetic drift

explanation.summary: Migration of genetically diverse individuals into a population is gene flow, which dilutes previously common alleles.
explanation.whyCorrect: Gene flow is the transfer of alleles between populations through migration and mating, and it increases genetic variation. As outsiders without the southern European thalassemia allele move in and have children, the frequency of that allele, and therefore the incidence of thalassemia minor, falls.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Assortative mating is preferential mating with similar individuals and would not systematically reduce a specific disease allele from outside migration.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The bottleneck effect is a sharp reduction in population size from a disaster; no catastrophic die-off occurred.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The founder effect describes a small separated group establishing a new, less diverse population; here diversity is increasing, not the reverse.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Genetic drift is random change in allele frequency by chance in small populations; the change here is driven by directed migration, not chance.

questions.topicName: Population Genetics

questions.stem: The Afrikaner population of South Africa descends largely from a small number of 17th-century Dutch colonists. Today this group has an unusually high frequency of the allele causing Huntington disease compared with the general European population. Which mechanism best accounts for this elevated frequency?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Founder effect

choices.label: B
choices.text: Gene flow

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mutation-selection equilibrium

choices.label: D
choices.text: Natural selection favoring the allele

choices.label: E
choices.text: Random mating

explanation.summary: When a new population is founded by a few individuals, alleles those founders happened to carry become overrepresented in descendants.
explanation.whyCorrect: The founder effect occurs when a small group separates from a larger population and founds a new one whose genotypes resemble that small group. Because some original Dutch colonists carried the Huntington allele, chance overrepresentation among the founders spread it through the isolated, growing community.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Gene flow introduces alleles from other populations and increases diversity; this scenario reflects isolation and descent from few founders.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mutation-selection equilibrium balances new deleterious mutations against their removal by selection and does not explain enrichment in one descended community.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Huntington disease is not associated with a reproductive advantage that natural selection would favor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Random mating alone does not raise the frequency of a specific allele; the key here is the limited founding gene pool.

questions.topicName: Population Genetics

questions.stem: A large population of beetles lives in a meadow. A person walking through the meadow unintentionally steps on and kills nearly all of the brown/green beetles in a single afternoon, leaving mostly tan beetles to reproduce. The next generation is overwhelmingly tan. Which term best describes this phenomenon?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Assortative mating

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bottleneck effect

choices.label: C
choices.text: Gene flow

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mendelian inheritance

choices.label: E
choices.text: Mutation-selection equilibrium

explanation.summary: A sudden, random event that sharply reduces population size and eliminates alleles is the bottleneck effect.
explanation.whyCorrect: The bottleneck effect is a sharp reduction in population size, and therefore in alleles, caused by an environmental event. The random destruction of most brown/green beetles rapidly decreased those alleles, producing genetic drift toward the tan allele and reduced overall genetic variation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Assortative mating is preferential mating with similar individuals, not death from a random event.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gene flow is movement of alleles between populations by migration; no migration occurred here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mendelian inheritance describes how offspring inherit parental alleles, not a sudden loss of individuals.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Mutation-selection equilibrium is a steady-state balance of mutation and selection, not an abrupt catastrophic loss.

questions.topicName: Population Genetics

questions.stem: In a population of 10,000 people that mates randomly, 400 individuals are affected by an autosomal recessive disorder. Assuming Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, approximately how many individuals in this population are unaffected carriers of the disease allele?

explanation.summary: Carrier count equals the heterozygote frequency 2pq multiplied by the total population.
explanation.whyCorrect: The affected are homozygous recessive, so q squared = 400/10,000 = 0.04 and q = 0.2. Then p = 1 - q = 0.8. Carriers are heterozygotes: 2pq = 2 x 0.8 x 0.2 = 0.32. Multiplying by 10,000 gives 3,200 carriers.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 400 is the number of affected homozygous recessive individuals, not the carriers.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 800 corresponds to using q (0.2) times... an incorrect setup and does not represent 2pq.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 1,600 results from omitting the factor of 2 and using pq (0.16) instead of 2pq.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 6,400 is p squared times the population (0.64 x 10,000), the number of homozygous dominant individuals, not carriers.

questions.topicName: Population Genetics

questions.stem: A student is applying the Hardy-Weinberg equation p squared + 2pq + q squared = 1 to a single gene with one dominant and one recessive allele. Which term of this equation represents the frequency of heterozygous individuals in the population?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 2pq

choices.label: B
choices.text: p

choices.label: C
choices.text: p squared

choices.label: D
choices.text: q

choices.label: E
choices.text: q squared

explanation.summary: In the Hardy-Weinberg equation, 2pq is the frequency of heterozygotes.
explanation.whyCorrect: The middle term 2pq represents the probability of inheriting one dominant and one recessive allele, which is the heterozygote. The factor of 2 accounts for the two ways a heterozygote can form, with the dominant allele coming from either the maternal or paternal side.

whyWrongByChoice.B: p is the frequency of the dominant allele, not a genotype frequency.
whyWrongByChoice.C: p squared is the frequency of homozygous dominant individuals.
whyWrongByChoice.D: q is the frequency of the recessive allele, not a genotype frequency.
whyWrongByChoice.E: q squared is the frequency of homozygous recessive individuals.

questions.topicName: Population Genetics

questions.stem: In several regions of the world where malaria is endemic, the recessive HbS allele of the beta-globin gene remains at a relatively high frequency, even though individuals who are homozygous (HbS/HbS) develop sickle cell disease and historically often died before reproducing. Which explanation best accounts for the persistence of this allele in these populations?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Assortative mating causes HbS carriers to preferentially mate with one another

choices.label: B
choices.text: Gene flow from non-malarial regions continually adds HbS alleles

choices.label: C
choices.text: Heterozygous carriers (HbA/HbS) have a survival advantage against severe malaria

choices.label: D
choices.text: Random genetic drift alone fixes the HbS allele in large populations

choices.label: E
choices.text: The HbS allele arose by a founder effect in every affected region

explanation.summary: Balancing natural selection maintains the HbS allele because heterozygotes resist the worst complications of malaria.
explanation.whyCorrect: The HbS allele can confer resistance to the worst complications of malaria in carriers with sickle cell trait (HbA/HbS). In malaria-endemic areas these heterozygotes are more likely to survive and reproduce, so natural selection maintains the allele despite the harm to homozygotes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The brick attributes persistence to a malaria-related survival advantage, not to carriers choosing one another as mates.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The allele is retained by selective pressure within malarial regions, not by import from non-malarial areas, which actually select against HbS.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Genetic drift is random and is a weaker force in large populations; it does not explain a directional survival advantage.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A founder effect independently producing the same allele in every malarial region is not the mechanism; selection explains its maintenance.

questions.topicName: Population Genetics

questions.stem: A researcher wants to model a gene using the Hardy-Weinberg principle, which requires the population to be in equilibrium. Which of the following is one of the assumptions that must hold for a population to remain in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Alleles frequently mutate from one generation to the next

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mating occurs randomly within the population

choices.label: C
choices.text: Strong natural selection favors one allele over another

choices.label: D
choices.text: The population is very small

choices.label: E
choices.text: There is ongoing immigration and emigration

explanation.summary: Random mating is a required assumption of Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium.
explanation.whyCorrect: The Hardy-Weinberg model assumes no selection, no mutation, a large population, random mating, and no migration. Random mating is therefore one of the necessary assumptions for the equation to hold.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Recurrent mutation changes allele frequencies over generations and is assumed not to occur.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Selection favoring one allele violates the assumption of no selective forces and shifts allele frequencies away from equilibrium.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A very small population makes genetic drift powerful; equilibrium assumes a population large enough that one new individual does not alter allele proportions.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Immigration and emigration introduce gene flow, which the model explicitly assumes is absent.

questions.topicName: Population Genetics

questions.stem: A couple seeks preconception genetic counseling for cystic fibrosis carrier screening. The counselor explains that the standard panel tests for the most common CFTR mutations, and that a negative result is more reassuring for the white-American partner (panel sensitivity about 71.9%) than it would be for a patient of Asian ancestry (panel sensitivity about 23.4%). Which statement best explains this difference?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cystic fibrosis is not a heritable condition in people of Asian ancestry and arises only sporadically

choices.label: B
choices.text: People of Asian ancestry cannot be carriers of CFTR mutations, so screening them is unnecessary

choices.label: C
choices.text: The CFTR gene is X-linked, so ancestry changes the inheritance pattern and the detection rate

choices.label: D
choices.text: The panel detects a smaller proportion of the disease-causing CFTR mutations present in people of Asian ancestry

choices.label: E
choices.text: The standard panel has 100% sensitivity in all ancestral groups and therefore misses no disease-causing mutations

explanation.summary: Carrier screening sensitivity depends on ancestry because the causative CFTR mutations differ between populations.
explanation.whyCorrect: Carrier rates and the specific CFTR mutations that cause cystic fibrosis are highly dependent on ancestry. The standard panel captures a lower fraction of the mutations found in Asian-American patients (23.4%) than in white-American patients (71.9%), so a negative result leaves a larger residual carrier risk and is less reassuring.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cystic fibrosis is an autosomal recessive heritable disease in all populations; it is not absent in any ancestry.
whyWrongByChoice.B: People of any ancestry can carry CFTR mutations; the panel simply detects fewer of them in this group.
whyWrongByChoice.C: CFTR is autosomal, not X-linked, and the inheritance pattern does not change with ancestry.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The panel does not have perfect sensitivity; the stated values (71.9% and 23.4%) show it misses some mutations.

questions.topicName: Population Genetics

questions.stem: A 6-month-old infant of Ashkenazi Jewish descent presents with developmental regression, exaggerated startle response, seizures, and a cherry-red spot on the macula. Deficiency of which enzyme is most likely responsible for this presentation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Alpha-galactosidase A

choices.label: B
choices.text: Glucocerebrosidase

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hexosaminidase A

choices.label: D
choices.text: Phenylalanine hydroxylase

choices.label: E
choices.text: The CFTR chloride channel

explanation.summary: Tay-Sachs disease results from hexosaminidase A deficiency and is more common in Ashkenazi Jews.
explanation.whyCorrect: Tay-Sachs disease results from a deficiency of the hexosaminidase A enzyme and causes seizures, a cherry-red macula, and other neurological deficits. It is found at higher rates in Ashkenazi Jews, consistent with this infant's ancestry and findings.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Alpha-galactosidase A deficiency causes Fabry disease, which does not present with a cherry-red macula in infancy.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Glucocerebrosidase deficiency is associated with Gaucher disease, a different autosomal recessive condition also enriched in Jewish populations but not marked by a cherry-red macula in this classic infantile pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency causes phenylketonuria, which is not the disorder described here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The CFTR chloride channel defect causes cystic fibrosis, a respiratory and digestive disease, not this neurodegenerative picture.

questions.topicName: Population Genetics

questions.stem: A woman with curly hair reports that she is romantically attracted only to men who also have curly hair. Considering the genetic concepts that cause populations to deviate from Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, this preference is an example of which phenomenon?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Assortative mating

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bottleneck effect

choices.label: C
choices.text: Gene flow

choices.label: D
choices.text: Genetic drift

choices.label: E
choices.text: Random mating

explanation.summary: Choosing mates who share a trait is assortative mating, a deviation from random mating.
explanation.whyCorrect: Assortative mating is the tendency of individuals to mate with others who are similar to them, which decreases random mating in a population. Preferring a partner who shares the curly-hair phenotype is phenotypic assortative mating.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The bottleneck effect is a sharp population reduction from a disaster, unrelated to mate choice.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gene flow is the movement of alleles between populations by migration.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Genetic drift is random change in allele frequency by chance, not a mating preference.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Random mating is the opposite of the described behavior; this woman is selecting mates nonrandomly by phenotype.

questions.topicName: Population Genetics

questions.stem: A genetics lecturer defines a term as the differences in DNA sequence for a specific gene at the same position on a chromosome, which can lead to diverse traits, disease risks, or medication responses within a population and influences features such as eye color. Which term is being described?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Allelic variation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bottleneck effect

choices.label: C
choices.text: Founder effect

choices.label: D
choices.text: Genetic drift

choices.label: E
choices.text: Mendelian inheritance

explanation.summary: Different forms of a gene at the same locus are allelic variation, the basis of genetic diversity.
explanation.whyCorrect: Allelic variation describes the presence of different alleles at a specific position (locus) on a chromosome. It contributes to overall genetic diversity within a population and underlies both normal traits, such as eye color, and disease risks or drug responses.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The bottleneck effect is a type of genetic drift that decreases diversity, not the definition of sequence differences at a locus.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The founder effect is also a type of genetic drift and reduces diversity in a new subpopulation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Genetic drift is random change in allele frequency by chance, not the definition of allele differences themselves.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Mendelian inheritance describes the random reassortment of parental alleles to form offspring genotypes, not the diversity of alleles at a locus.

questions.topicName: Population Genetics

questions.stem: A harmful recessive allele that causes disease only in homozygotes persists in a large population at a low, stable frequency across many generations. Affected homozygotes are removed from the breeding population each generation, yet the allele does not disappear because new copies keep arising. Which population-genetics concept best describes this stable balance?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Assortative mating between similar individuals

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bottleneck effect from a sudden population reduction

choices.label: C
choices.text: Founder effect in a newly founded population

choices.label: D
choices.text: Gene flow between neighboring populations

choices.label: E
choices.text: Mutation-selection equilibrium

explanation.summary: A balance between new deleterious mutations and their removal by selection is the mutation-selection equilibrium.
explanation.whyCorrect: The mutation-selection equilibrium is a state in which the rate of creation of deleterious alleles by mutation is balanced by the rate of their elimination by selection. This balance helps maintain genetic variation, keeping the harmful allele at a low but stable frequency.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Assortative mating is preferential mating with similar individuals and does not describe a mutation-selection balance.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The bottleneck effect is a sudden population reduction from a disaster, not a steady equilibrium.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The founder effect involves a small group founding a new population, not an ongoing mutation-versus-selection balance.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Gene flow is migration of alleles between populations and would change frequencies rather than hold them stable through mutation and selection.

questions.topicName: Population Genetics

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man is started on carbamazepine for focal seizures. Within the first week of therapy he develops a rapidly spreading painful rash with mucosal involvement and skin blistering, and the reaction is thought to be immune-mediated. Which of the following pharmacogenetic findings most likely explains this adverse drug reaction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: CYP2D6*2

choices.label: C
choices.text: TPMT*2, *3

choices.label: D
choices.text: CYP3A4*17

explanation.summary: Certain HLA alleles predispose to severe cutaneous hypersensitivity reactions to specific drugs.
explanation.whyCorrect: Alleles of the human leukocyte antigen (HLA) system are associated with idiosyncratic, delayed hypersensitivity adverse drug reactions such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis. Carbamazepine-triggered severe cutaneous reactions are linked to HLA variants (HLA-B*15:02), so this genotype best explains an immune-mediated blistering rash appearing shortly after starting the drug.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CYP2D6 variants alter oxidative Phase 1 metabolism of drugs such as antidepressants; they change drug levels rather than trigger an HLA-mediated immune skin reaction.
whyWrongByChoice.B: DRD2 dopamine receptor variants affect antipsychotic efficacy and weight gain, not carbamazepine hypersensitivity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: TPMT deficiency causes myelosuppression with thiopurines (azathioprine, 6-mercaptopurine), not carbamazepine-associated skin reactions.
whyWrongByChoice.D: CYP3A4 reduced-function variants slow metabolism of drugs like tacrolimus and cyclosporine, causing accumulation and toxicity, not an immune cutaneous reaction.

questions.topicName: Pharmacogenetics: An Introduction

questions.stem: A woman with uncontrolled hypertension is about to add metoprolol to her regimen. Her pharmacogenetic panel reveals the ADRB1 Arg389Gly (R389G) receptor variant, which is reported to increase the efficacy of metoprolol. Which of the following is the most appropriate parameter to monitor for this patient's response to therapy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Asthma exacerbation frequency

choices.label: B
choices.text: Blood pressure

choices.label: C
choices.text: Body weight

choices.label: D
choices.text: Serum cholesterol level

choices.label: E
choices.text: Short-term memory

explanation.summary: Monitoring should target the intended therapeutic effect of the drug given the receptor variant.
explanation.whyCorrect: Metoprolol is a beta-1 adrenergic antagonist used to lower blood pressure, and the ADRB1 R389G variant is reported to alter the antihypertensive response at the beta-1 receptor. Because the drug is being used to control hypertension, blood pressure is the parameter that directly reflects efficacy and should be monitored.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Asthma exacerbation risk relates to beta-2 receptor (ADRB2) variants and beta-agonist therapy, not the beta-1 ADRB1 variant.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Weight gain is associated with dopamine D2 receptor variants and antipsychotic therapy, not with a beta-1 receptor variant and metoprolol.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cholesterol is not the therapeutic target of a beta-blocker used for blood pressure control and does not reflect the ADRB1 variant effect.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Memory change is linked to certain serotonin receptor variants with escitalopram, not to a beta-1 receptor variant.

questions.topicName: Pharmacogenetics: An Introduction

questions.stem: A genetics lecture reviews how variation in DNA sequence among individuals underlies differences in drug response. Genetic polymorphism refers to the presence of two or more variant forms of a DNA sequence in a population. Which of the following is the most common cause of these genetic variants?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Advancing age of the patient

choices.label: B
choices.text: Multiple-nucleotide insertion polymorphism

choices.label: C
choices.text: Multiple-nucleotide deletion polymorphism in a coding segment

choices.label: D
choices.text: Obesity and increased body fat

choices.label: E
choices.text: Single-nucleotide polymorphisms

explanation.summary: The most common type of genetic polymorphism is a single-nucleotide change.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that the most common type of polymorphism involves variation at a single nucleotide (for example, A to G) in the DNA sequence, also called a single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP). SNPs can occur in coding, non-coding, or regulatory regions of genes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Age influences drug metabolism and excretion but is not a cause of genetic variants.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Addition of multiple nucleotides (insertions) is a form of variation but is not the most common type of polymorphism.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Deletion of multiple nucleotides occurs but is far less common than single-nucleotide variation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Obesity is a non-genetic factor that can affect drug distribution and clearance; it is not a cause of DNA sequence variants.

questions.topicName: Pharmacogenetics: An Introduction

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman with Crohn disease is started on azathioprine. Two weeks later she develops profound leukopenia, anemia, and easy bruising. Genotyping shows she carries TPMT*2 and *3 alleles. Which of the following best explains her bone marrow toxicity?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An HLA-mediated immune reaction destroys marrow precursors

choices.label: B
choices.text: Decreased inactivation of 6-mercaptopurine

choices.label: C
choices.text: Enhanced renal excretion reduces drug half-life

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased beta-endorphin binding at opioid receptors

choices.label: E
choices.text: Increased methylation accelerates clearance of the active drug

explanation.summary: TPMT deficiency reduces inactivation of thiopurines, leading to toxic accumulation and myelosuppression.
explanation.whyCorrect: Thiopurine S-methyltransferase (TPMT) is a Phase 2 enzyme that methylates and inactivates thiopurine drugs. Defects in the TPMT gene lead to decreased methylation and decreased inactivation of 6-mercaptopurine, so cytotoxic metabolites accumulate and cause enhanced bone marrow toxicity with myelosuppression, anemia, leukopenia, and bleeding tendency.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The mechanism here is impaired drug inactivation and metabolite accumulation, not an HLA immune reaction.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The toxicity results from reduced enzymatic inactivation, not enhanced renal excretion, which would lower drug exposure.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Beta-endorphin binding relates to the OPRM1 opioid receptor variant, unrelated to thiopurine toxicity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: TPMT variants decrease, not increase, methylation; increased methylation would inactivate the drug and reduce toxicity.

questions.topicName: Pharmacogenetics: An Introduction

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man with reflux esophagitis reports no symptom relief after weeks of a standard-dose proton pump inhibitor. Genotyping reveals CYP2C19*1/*17, classifying him as an ultra-rapid metabolizer. Which of the following best explains his treatment failure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Increased enzyme activity clears the drug before it can act

choices.label: B
choices.text: The drug accumulates to toxic levels and inhibits its own target

choices.label: C
choices.text: The variant alters the proton pump so the drug cannot bind

choices.label: D
choices.text: The variant blocks intestinal absorption of the drug

choices.label: E
choices.text: The variant triggers an immune hypersensitivity reaction

explanation.summary: Increased-function CYP2C19 variants speed drug metabolism, reducing drug exposure and efficacy.
explanation.whyCorrect: The CYP2C19*17 variant increases the enzyme's ability to metabolize drugs, and two copies produce an ultra-rapid metabolizer phenotype. Increased metabolism of proton pump inhibitors leads to loss of drug effectiveness, and a higher dose may be needed to achieve a therapeutic effect.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Ultra-rapid metabolism lowers drug levels rather than causing toxic accumulation; accumulation occurs with poor metabolizers.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The variant affects the metabolizing enzyme, not the structure of the proton pump target.
whyWrongByChoice.D: CYP2C19 governs hepatic metabolism, not intestinal absorption of the drug.
whyWrongByChoice.E: This is a metabolic (pharmacokinetic) effect, not an HLA-mediated immune reaction.

questions.topicName: Pharmacogenetics: An Introduction

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man is started on low-dose venlafaxine for anxiety. After 8 days he reports that although the drug helped somewhat, he did not feel like himself and had troubling side effects, so he stopped it. A pharmacogenetic panel returns a CYP2D6 *4/*10 genotype. Which of the following best describes his metabolizer status and its effect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Enhanced drug transporter uptake increasing efficacy

choices.label: B
choices.text: Immune sensitization causing a hypersensitivity reaction

choices.label: C
choices.text: Intermediate metabolizer with reduced drug clearance

choices.label: D
choices.text: Normal metabolizer requiring no dose change

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ultra-rapid metabolizer with subtherapeutic drug levels

explanation.summary: Reduced-function CYP2D6 genotypes produce an intermediate metabolizer with higher drug exposure and adverse effects.
explanation.whyCorrect: The CYP2D6 *4/*10 genotype predicts reduced or intermediate metabolizer status. Reduced CYP2D6 function decreases metabolism of venlafaxine (and affects roughly 25% of commonly prescribed drugs), so the drug is cleared more slowly and adverse effects are more likely, which explains why the patient did not feel like himself.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CYP2D6 is a metabolizing enzyme, not a drug transporter, and reduced function decreases rather than enhances clearance.
whyWrongByChoice.B: His symptoms reflect a pharmacokinetic metabolizer effect, not an HLA-type immune hypersensitivity reaction.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The *4/*10 genotype reduces enzyme function, so this is not a normal metabolizer requiring no change.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ultra-rapid metabolizers clear drug quickly and tend to have subtherapeutic levels; the *4/*10 genotype produces the opposite, reduced metabolism.

questions.topicName: Pharmacogenetics: An Introduction

questions.stem: A 52-year-old kidney transplant recipient maintained on tacrolimus is found to carry a CYP3A4 decreased-function variant (CYP3A4*8). Which of the following outcomes is most likely if the standard dose is used without adjustment?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An HLA-mediated skin reaction

choices.label: B
choices.text: Elevated tacrolimus levels and drug toxicity

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased risk of asthma exacerbation

choices.label: D
choices.text: No change in tacrolimus levels

choices.label: E
choices.text: Subtherapeutic tacrolimus levels and graft rejection

explanation.summary: Decreased-function metabolizing enzyme variants raise drug levels and toxicity risk for narrow-therapeutic-index drugs.
explanation.whyCorrect: Decreased-function CYP3A4 variants (such as *8, *11, *13) reduce metabolism of drugs like cyclosporine and tacrolimus. Slower clearance leads to drug accumulation and toxicity, which is especially dangerous for immunosuppressants with a narrow therapeutic index.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CYP3A4 variants act through metabolism, not HLA-mediated immune skin reactions.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Asthma exacerbation risk relates to beta-2 receptor variants, not CYP3A4 metabolism.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A decreased-function variant does change pharmacokinetics, increasing exposure.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Reduced metabolism raises, not lowers, drug levels, so subtherapeutic levels and rejection would be unexpected.

questions.topicName: Pharmacogenetics: An Introduction

questions.stem: Before prescribing abacavir to a patient with HIV, a clinician orders pharmacogenetic screening. The result is positive for HLA-B*57:01. Which of the following is the most appropriate reason to avoid abacavir in this patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Abacavir will accumulate due to reduced Phase 1 metabolism

choices.label: B
choices.text: The drug transporter variant will block cellular uptake

choices.label: C
choices.text: The patient is at high risk of a drug hypersensitivity reaction

choices.label: D
choices.text: The patient will be an ultra-rapid metabolizer of abacavir

choices.label: E
choices.text: The variant reduces abacavir binding to its target

explanation.summary: HLA-B*57:01 predicts an immune-mediated hypersensitivity reaction to abacavir.
explanation.whyCorrect: The HLA-B*57:01 allele is associated with an activated immune reaction, a hypersensitivity reaction to the drug abacavir. Because HLA alleles drive idiosyncratic, immune-mediated adverse reactions, carrying this allele is a reason to avoid abacavir and use an alternative.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The concern is an HLA-driven immune reaction, not reduced Phase 1 metabolism and accumulation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: HLA molecules present antigens to immune cells; they are not drug transporters affecting uptake.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HLA alleles determine immune recognition, not metabolizer status; abacavir risk here is immunologic, not metabolic.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The reaction reflects immune activation, not altered drug binding to a pharmacologic target.

questions.topicName: Pharmacogenetics: An Introduction

questions.stem: A pharmacogenomics researcher identifies a SNP located outside of a gene that reliably correlates with response to a particular drug but has no effect on protein production or function. Which of the following best classifies this SNP?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Coding SNP

choices.label: B
choices.text: Copy number variation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Frameshift variant

choices.label: D
choices.text: Linked (indicative) SNP

choices.label: E
choices.text: Noncoding (causative) SNP within the gene

explanation.summary: SNPs outside a gene that correlate with a trait without changing protein are linked (indicative) SNPs.
explanation.whyCorrect: Linked SNPs, also called indicative SNPs, occur outside the gene and have no effect on protein production or function, yet they may correlate with drug response or a certain disease. This matches a marker outside the gene that predicts drug response without altering the protein.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A coding SNP lies within the coding region and changes the amino acid sequence, so it does affect the protein.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A copy number variation is a deletion or duplication of a DNA segment, not a single-nucleotide marker outside the gene.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A frameshift variant is a loss-of-function change within the coding sequence that alters the protein, not a non-functional marker.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A noncoding causative SNP lies inside the gene and changes the amount of protein produced, unlike this marker.

questions.topicName: Pharmacogenetics: An Introduction

questions.stem: A student is asked to distinguish pharmacogenetics from pharmacogenomics. Which of the following statements most accurately describes pharmacogenetics?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It analyzes the complete set of proteins expressed in a cell or tissue sample

choices.label: B
choices.text: It examines multi-gene interactions across the whole genome and their drug effects

choices.label: C
choices.text: It measures the full set of metabolites produced in a cell or tissue

choices.label: D
choices.text: It studies how a person's entire genome influences the response to medications

choices.label: E
choices.text: It studies how variations in a single gene affect response to a specific drug

explanation.summary: Pharmacogenetics focuses on single-gene variants and their effect on drug response.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines pharmacogenetics as the study of how variations in a single gene affect an individual's response to a specific drug. Pharmacogenomics takes the broader approach of looking at how the entire genome and multi-gene interactions influence response to medications.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Analyzing the full set of proteins is proteomics, not pharmacogenetics.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Studying multi-gene interactions across the genome is pharmacogenomics, not the single-gene focus of pharmacogenetics.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Measuring the full set of metabolites is metabolomics, not pharmacogenetics.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This describes pharmacogenomics, the broader whole-genome approach, not pharmacogenetics.

questions.topicName: Pharmacogenetics: An Introduction

questions.stem: A review of G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) as drug targets notes that roughly a third of FDA-approved drugs act through them and that GPCR drug targets are frequently affected by a particular kind of variant. Which of the following types of mutation most commonly affects GPCR drug targets?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Balanced reciprocal translocation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Missense mutations

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mitochondrial DNA depletion

choices.label: D
choices.text: Trinucleotide repeat expansion

choices.label: E
choices.text: Whole-chromosome aneuploidy

explanation.summary: GPCR drug targets are most often affected by missense mutations.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that GPCR drug targets are often affected by missense mutations, followed by loss-of-function changes from nonsense or frameshift mutations and by copy number variations. The results can include decreased ligand binding, modified G protein selectivity, or altered expression, localization, trafficking, or desensitization.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Balanced translocations are structural chromosomal changes, not the missense mutations most often affecting GPCRs.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mitochondrial DNA depletion is unrelated to the missense variants that affect GPCR drug targets.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Trinucleotide repeat expansions cause other disorders and are not the described GPCR target variant.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Whole-chromosome aneuploidy is not described as the common variant affecting GPCR drug targets.

questions.topicName: Pharmacogenetics: An Introduction

questions.stem: A clinical genetics report describes a genomic change as a variant that may increase a person's risk of developing a condition, disorder, or disease. According to the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics classification, which of the following terms best describes this variant?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Benign variant

choices.label: B
choices.text: Likely benign variant

choices.label: C
choices.text: Pathogenic variant

choices.label: D
choices.text: Silent (synonymous) variant

choices.label: E
choices.text: Variant of uncertain significance

explanation.summary: A variant that increases disease risk is classified as pathogenic.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines a pathogenic variant as a genomic variant that may increase a person's risk of developing a condition, disorder, or disease. The ACMG classification system applies the modifiers pathogenic, likely pathogenic, uncertain significance, likely benign, and benign to describe how a change may impact gene function.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A benign variant has little to no effect and does not increase disease risk.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A likely benign variant is probably harmless and is not described as increasing disease risk.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Silent or synonymous is a molecular description of a coding change and is not one of the ACMG clinical significance categories used here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A variant of uncertain significance has insufficient evidence to classify its impact, so it is not defined as increasing risk.

questions.topicName: Pharmacogenetics: An Introduction

questions.stem: A research team supporting a precision medicine program is assembling several molecular biology datasets on the same cohort. One arm of the project catalogs the RNA composition of sampled cells. Which of the following branches of molecular biology is this arm of the project performing?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Genomics

choices.label: B
choices.text: Metabolomics

choices.label: C
choices.text: Pharmacogenetics

choices.label: D
choices.text: Proteomics

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transcriptomics

explanation.summary: Transcriptomics is the branch of molecular biology that describes RNA composition.
explanation.whyCorrect: Precision medicine draws on several molecular biology disciplines, each defined by the class of molecule it profiles. Transcriptomics is defined as the study of RNA composition, so cataloging the RNA content of sampled cells is transcriptomic work.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Genomics addresses DNA structure and function rather than the RNA present in a cell.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Metabolomics profiles cellular metabolites, not transcripts.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pharmacogenetics addresses interactions of drugs with an individual's genetic makeup, not RNA cataloging.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Proteomics describes protein composition, a different class of molecule from RNA.

questions.topicName: Pharmacogenetics: An Introduction

questions.stem: A health system is launching a precision medicine initiative and must decide which data to gather on each enrolled patient. Which of the following best describes the data that define the precision medicine approach?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Clinical, lifestyle, genetic, and biomarker information

choices.label: B
choices.text: Family pedigree drawn over three generations only

choices.label: C
choices.text: Population-level incidence and prevalence statistics

choices.label: D
choices.text: Prescription refill history and pharmacy claims data

choices.label: E
choices.text: Signs and symptoms plus standard test results alone

explanation.summary: Precision medicine collects and analyzes large-scale clinical, lifestyle, genetic, and biomarker data.
explanation.whyCorrect: Precision medicine is a novel clinical approach that collects and analyzes large-scale data, including clinical, lifestyle, genetic, and biomarker information, and applies it to diagnosis and treatment. This contrasts with the traditional approach in which treatment rests on the one-drug-fits-all concept.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A pedigree is only one narrow slice of family history and omits the lifestyle and biomarker data required.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Population incidence and prevalence figures describe groups rather than the individual-level data precision medicine uses.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Refill and claims data are not the categories that define the precision medicine dataset.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Evaluating patients by signs and symptoms plus standard tests is the traditional approach precision medicine is meant to extend.

questions.topicName: Pharmacogenetics: An Introduction

questions.stem: A pharmacology lecture reviews how a patient's genetic makeup can influence the movement of a drug through the body. Although every pharmacokinetic step can in principle be affected, two are affected most often. Which of the following pairs of pharmacokinetic processes is most often altered by genetic variation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Absorption and distribution

choices.label: B
choices.text: Absorption and excretion

choices.label: C
choices.text: Distribution and metabolism

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ingestion and absorption

choices.label: E
choices.text: Metabolism and excretion

explanation.summary: Genetic variation most often affects drug metabolism and excretion.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pharmacokinetics covers absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion. Each of these can be affected by a patient's genetic makeup, but metabolism and excretion are the steps most often affected, which is why genotype matters when choosing an appropriate medication and dose for a specific patient.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Absorption and distribution can be influenced by genotype but are not the steps most often affected.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Excretion is correctly included, but absorption is not the other process most often affected.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Metabolism is correctly included, but distribution is not the other process most often affected.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ingestion is the route of administration rather than a pharmacokinetic process altered by genotype.

questions.topicName: Pharmacogenetics: An Introduction

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman with persistent wheezing and reversible airflow obstruction on spirometry is being considered for a long-acting beta-agonist (LABA) as add-on therapy. Genotyping shows she carries the ADRB2 variant rs1042713 (R16G). Which of the following outcomes is she at increased risk for on this therapy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Asthma exacerbation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Blistering skin rash

choices.label: C
choices.text: Memory loss

choices.label: D
choices.text: Myelosuppression

choices.label: E
choices.text: Weight gain
